title: Houmuwu ding
creator: chinese-bronze-casters
type: Cast bronze ritual vessel
note: The heaviest bronze vessel to survive from the ancient world, cast for the Shang royal house at Anyang.
description: This massive rectangular cauldron (ding), weighing about 830 kilograms, was found in 1939 near Anyang, the last capital of the Shang dynasty; villagers reburied it to hide it from the Japanese army, and it was recovered in 1946. The inscription inside, read as Hou Mu Wu, dedicates it to a royal mother, probably a consort of King Wu Ding. Such vessels held offerings of meat to the ancestors. It was cast in a set of clay moulds, with handles added in a separate pour, and its sides are framed with taotie masks and dragons. The scale of the casting, requiring hundreds of workers to melt and pour the metal at once, shows the organising power of the Shang state, and the vessel has become a national symbol of Chinese antiquity.
image_file: HouMuWuDingFullView.jpg
image_caption: Houmuwu ding, National Museum of China

title: Bronze heads and masks from Sanxingdui
creator: chinese-bronze-casters
type: Cast bronze, some with gold foil
note: Strange, wide-eyed bronze heads and masks from two sacrificial pits that revealed an unknown Bronze Age civilisation in Sichuan.
description: In 1986 workers at Sanxingdui near Chengdu uncovered two pits filled with deliberately broken and burned objects: elephant tusks, jades, a bronze tree nearly four metres tall, a standing figure of 2.6 metres, and dozens of life-size bronze heads, some covered with gold foil masks, along with huge masks with protruding cylindrical eyes. Six more pits excavated from 2019 have added many more finds. The objects were cast with the same piece-mould technology as Shang bronzes, but their imagery has no parallel in the Yellow River valley, and no writing explains them. They probably represent ancestors or deities of a kingdom of the ancient Shu people. Sanxingdui transformed the picture of early China, showing that the Bronze Age had several centres.
image_file: Gold Mask (黄金面罩).jpg
image_caption: Gold mask from Sanxingdui

title: Four-Ram Square Zun
creator: chinese-bronze-casters
type: Cast bronze wine vessel
note: A Shang wine vessel with four rams modelled in the round at its corners, among the finest castings of the Bronze Age.
description: This square wine vessel was found in 1938 by farmers in Ningxiang county, Hunan, far south of the Shang heartland. Its upper part is a flaring square mouth, and its body is formed by four rams whose heads and forelegs project from the corners, their horns curling round their faces; dragons rear up between them. The heads and horns were cast separately and then locked into the main mould, a complex procedure that shows the skill of southern bronze casters, who may have worked in a distinct regional tradition. The vessel was damaged in wartime and restored in the 1950s. It is one of the most celebrated of all Chinese bronzes, combining abstract surface decoration with sculptural animals.
image_file: Square zun with four sheep 01.jpg
image_caption: Four-Ram Square Zun, National Museum of China

title: Mao Gong ding
creator: chinese-bronze-casters
type: Cast bronze ritual vessel with inscription
note: A Western Zhou tripod cauldron whose inscription of nearly 500 characters is the longest on any ancient Chinese bronze.
description: Found in Shaanxi province in the 1840s, the Mao Gong ding is a plain, round three-legged cauldron of the late Western Zhou period. Its importance lies in the inscription of 497 characters cast inside the bowl, in which a Zhou king, probably King Xuan, charges the Duke of Mao with governing the realm, warns him against abuses and lists rich gifts of chariots, robes and weapons. The duke then records that he made the vessel to commemorate the honour. The text is a key source for Zhou government and an admired model of bronze script (jinwen), studied by calligraphers such as Wu Changshuo. The vessel passed through several private collections before reaching the National Palace Museum in Taipei.
image_file: Ding cauldron of Duke Mao.jpg
image_caption: Mao Gong ding, National Palace Museum, Taipei

title: Bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng
creator: chinese-bronze-casters
type: Set of 65 cast bronze bells
note: A set of 65 bronze bells hung on a three-tiered frame, buried with a Warring States ruler and still playable today.
description: In 1978 the tomb of Marquis Yi, ruler of the small state of Zeng, was excavated at Suizhou in Hubei. Among more than 15,000 objects was a complete orchestra, including this set of 65 bronze bells hanging from a lacquered wooden frame supported by bronze figures of warriors. Each bell, because of its almond-shaped cross-section, produces two different notes depending on where it is struck. Inscriptions in gold on the bells name the notes and the relations between the tuning systems of different states, giving unique evidence for ancient Chinese music theory. The set covers a range of five octaves. Its discovery showed the astonishing technical precision of Warring States casters, and replicas are used in concerts.
image_file: 湖北博物館曾侯乙編鐘.jpg
image_caption: The bells of Marquis Yi, Hubei Provincial Museum

title: Terracotta Army
creator: qin-terracotta-workshops
type: Painted terracotta figures
location: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor, Lintong, Xi'an
note: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers, horses and chariots buried in pits to guard the tomb of the First Emperor of Qin.
description: In 1974 farmers digging a well near Xi'an found fragments of clay figures, and archaeologists uncovered three pits east of the burial mound of Qin Shi Huang, who died in 210 BC. Pit 1 alone holds an army of an estimated six thousand soldiers in battle formation, with archers, infantry, chariots and officers; in total about eight thousand figures are thought to have been buried. They were made in workshops from moulded parts and individually finished heads, painted in bright colours and armed with real bronze weapons, many of which were looted soon after the emperor's death, when the pits were burned. The army reflects the emperor's belief that his power would continue in the afterlife. Excavation continues, and the emperor's tomb itself has not been opened.
image_file: 51714-Terracota-Army.jpg
image_caption: Soldiers in Pit 1 of the Terracotta Army

title: Flying Horse of Gansu
creator: han-tomb-artisans
type: Cast bronze
note: A bronze horse galloping with one hoof resting on a swallow, found in an Eastern Han tomb at Wuwei.
description: This small bronze horse, about 35 centimetres high, was found in 1969 in a tomb at Leitai in Wuwei, Gansu, along with a procession of bronze horses, chariots and riders. The horse races forward with three hooves in the air, balanced on a fourth that rests on a flying bird, a brilliant solution to the problem of showing speed in sculpture. It probably represents one of the 'heavenly horses' from Central Asia prized by Han rulers. Its identity has been debated: the bird is usually called a swallow, but some argue it is a falcon or the horse is a mythical creature. Chosen in 1983 as the symbol of Chinese tourism, it is one of the most famous objects of Chinese art.
image_file: Gansu Museum 2007 257.jpg
image_caption: Flying Horse of Gansu, Gansu Provincial Museum

title: Jade burial suit of Liu Sheng
creator: han-tomb-artisans
type: Jade plaques sewn with gold wire
note: A full-body suit of more than 2,400 jade plaques joined with gold wire, made for a Han prince in the belief that jade preserved the body.
description: Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan and a brother of Emperor Wu of Han, died in 113 BC and was buried with his wife Dou Wan in rock-cut tombs at Mancheng in Hebei, excavated in 1968. Both were clothed in suits of jade, Liu Sheng's made of 2,498 thin plaques cut to fit the shape of head, body, hands and feet and sewn together with about a kilogram of gold wire. Han texts describe such suits as a privilege of emperors and high nobles, worn in the hope that jade would keep the body from decay; in fact the bodies had turned to dust. Making one required years of work by skilled lapidaries. These were the first complete jade suits ever found and caused a sensation.
image_file: Jade burial suit of Liu Sheng.jpg
image_caption: Jade burial suit of Liu Sheng, Hebei Museum

title: Changxin Palace Lamp
creator: han-tomb-artisans
type: Gilt bronze lamp
note: A gilt-bronze lamp in the form of a kneeling servant girl, designed so that the smoke passes up her sleeve into her hollow body.
description: This lamp was found in 1968 in the Mancheng tomb of Dou Wan, wife of Liu Sheng. Inscriptions show that it had belonged to the household of the Changxin Palace, the residence of the empress dowager, before passing to the prince's family. A kneeling young woman holds the lamp in one hand while her other arm and sleeve form a chimney, which carries smoke into the hollow body and kept the room clean. Sliding panels let the light be adjusted in direction and brightness, and the parts can be taken apart for cleaning. The calm, natural figure and the clever engineering make it one of the best-known works of Han art.
image_file: Changxin Palace Lamp (11867682066).jpg
image_caption: Changxin Palace Lamp, Hebei Museum

title: T-shaped silk banner from Mawangdui Tomb 1
creator: han-tomb-artisans
type: Ink and colour on silk
note: A painted silk banner from the tomb of Lady Dai, showing the heavens, the earthly world and the underworld.
description: The tombs at Mawangdui in Changsha, excavated in 1972–74, belonged to the family of the Marquis of Dai. Tomb 1 contained the remarkably preserved body of Xin Zhui, Lady Dai, who died around 168 BC, and draped over her innermost coffin was this T-shaped silk banner about two metres long. At the top, in the heavens, are the sun with a crow, the moon with a toad and a serpent-bodied deity; in the middle the elderly lady herself, leaning on a staff, is attended by servants; below, offerings are laid out for her, and an underworld figure holds up the earth. The banner probably served in the funeral and may have guided her soul. It is one of the earliest major Chinese paintings to survive.
image_file: Mawangdui silk banner from tomb no1.jpg
image_caption: Silk banner from Mawangdui Tomb 1, Hunan Museum

title: Admonitions Scroll
creator: gu-kaizhi
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: The oldest surviving Chinese handscroll painting, illustrating a text on the proper conduct of court ladies.
description: The Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies was a poem written by Zhang Hua around 292 to criticise the behaviour of Empress Jia. The scroll illustrates it in a series of scenes separated by passages of text: Lady Feng throwing herself in front of a bear to protect the emperor, a lady at her mirror, a husband turning away from his wife in bed. Traditionally attributed to Gu Kaizhi, it is now generally thought to be a copy made between the fifth and seventh centuries, preserving an early composition. The figures are drawn with a fine, even line. The scroll entered the Qianlong Emperor's collection and was taken from Beijing by a British officer in 1900; it is now kept in the British Museum and shown only rarely.
image_file: Ku K'ai-chih 001.jpg
image_caption: Admonitions Scroll (detail), British Museum

title: Nymph of the Luo River
creator: gu-kaizhi
year: Song-dynasty copy of a composition attributed to Gu Kaizhi
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
location: Palace Museum, Beijing (other versions in Liaoning and Washington)
note: An illustration of Cao Zhi's poem about a prince's meeting with a river goddess, one of the most famous early Chinese paintings.
description: In his rhapsody of 222, the poet Cao Zhi describes stopping by the Luo River on his way home, seeing a beautiful goddess and falling in love with her, only for her to depart because humans and spirits cannot unite. The painting follows the poem from right to left: the prince on the bank, the nymph appearing over the water, her departure in a chariot drawn by dragons, and the prince's sorrowful journey home. Mountains and trees are small and archaic, like stage scenery, as in early Chinese painting. Several versions survive, all thought to be Song copies of a lost original associated with Gu Kaizhi. The work became a classic subject and is important evidence for early figure and landscape painting.
image_file: Gu Kaizhi-Nymph of the Luo River (full), Palace Museum, Beijing.jpg
image_caption: Nymph of the Luo River, Song copy, Palace Museum, Beijing

title: Preface to the Poems Composed at the Orchid Pavilion (Lantingji Xu)
creator: wang-xizhi
type: Calligraphy in running script; handscroll copies
note: The most celebrated work of Chinese calligraphy, known through Tang tracing copies after the original was buried with Emperor Taizong.
description: On the third day of the third month of 353, Wang Xizhi and forty-one friends gathered at the Orchid Pavilion near Shaoxing for a spring purification festival, floating wine cups on a winding stream and composing poems. Wang wrote a preface to the collection, 324 characters reflecting on the pleasure of the day and the brevity of life. Written spontaneously and with corrections, the manuscript was treasured by his descendants until, according to tradition, Emperor Taizong of Tang obtained it and had it buried with him. Taizong ordered court calligraphers to make copies, and the version known as the Shenlong copy, perhaps by Feng Chengsu, is thought closest to the original. The text has been copied by calligraphers ever since, and the gathering itself became a favourite subject of painting.
image_file: XingshuLantingxv.jpg
image_caption: Tang tracing copy of the Lantingji Xu

title: Colossal Buddha of Yungang Cave 20
creator: chinese-cave-temple-artists
type: Sandstone, carved in the cliff
note: A 14-metre seated Buddha carved for the Northern Wei emperors, now standing in the open after its cave front collapsed.
description: Around 460 the monk Tanyao persuaded the Northern Wei emperor Wencheng to sponsor five great caves at Wuzhou Mountain near the capital Pingcheng, today Datong, in part as atonement for an earlier persecution of Buddhism. Each cave held a colossal Buddha, and tradition links the five to the dynasty's emperors. The front wall of Cave 20 collapsed long ago, leaving its seated Buddha open to view. The broad shoulders, long ears, almond eyes and stylised robe draped over one shoulder show Central Asian and Indian influence, filtered through the Turkic-speaking Tuoba rulers. The Yungang site eventually contained over 250 caves and some 51,000 images, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Great.Buddha.Datong.jpg
image_caption: Colossal seated Buddha, Yungang Grottoes

title: Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple, Longmen
creator: chinese-cave-temple-artists
type: Limestone, carved in the cliff
note: A 17-metre Buddha carved under Emperor Gaozong with funds from Empress Wu, the supreme monument of Tang sculpture.
description: Longmen, south of Luoyang where the Yi River runs between two limestone cliffs, holds more than 2,000 caves and niches carved from the late fifth to the eighth century. The largest group, the open-air Fengxian Temple, was completed in 675. An inscription records that Empress Wu, later the only woman to rule China in her own name, contributed money from her cosmetics allowance. The central Vairocana, the cosmic Buddha of the Huayan school, is about 17 metres high and is flanked by disciples, bodhisattvas, heavenly kings and fierce guardians. Its calm, full face and soft, rounded form represent the mature Tang style, which spread to Korea and Japan. Popular tradition says the Buddha's face was modelled on the empress herself.
image_file: Ancient Buddhist Grottoes at Longmen- Fengxian Temple, Colossal Statue of Vairocana.jpg
image_caption: Vairocana Buddha, Fengxian Temple, Longmen

title: Murals of the Mogao Caves
creator: chinese-cave-temple-artists
type: Mineral pigments on plaster; painted clay sculpture
note: About 45,000 square metres of Buddhist murals in nearly 500 caves at the Silk Road oasis of Dunhuang.
description: According to an inscription, the monk Lezun began cutting the first cave at Mogao in 366, and for a thousand years monks, merchants and officials sponsored new caves in the cliff near the oasis of Dunhuang, a meeting point of Chinese, Central Asian and Indian cultures. The walls are painted with Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives, huge paradise scenes of the Pure Land with palaces and dancers, landscapes, portraits of donors and scenes of daily life, while clay sculptures fill the niches. Because almost all Tang painting elsewhere has been lost, the murals are the best evidence for it. In 1900 a sealed library cave was found, and many manuscripts and paintings were taken abroad by Aurel Stein, Paul Pelliot and others. Mogao is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Mogao Cave 220 Tang Dynasty emperor and officials 莫高窟220窟东壁门北 初唐君臣帝王.jpg
image_caption: Emperor and officials, early Tang mural, Mogao Cave 220

title: Pensive Bodhisattva (National Treasure No. 83)
creator: korean-buddhist-sculptors
type: Gilt bronze
note: A gilt-bronze bodhisattva seated in meditation with one leg crossed, a masterpiece of Three Kingdoms Korean sculpture.
description: The pensive pose, with the right leg crossed over the left knee and the fingers of the right hand lightly touching the cheek, was popular in East Asian Buddhism in the sixth and seventh centuries, often identified with Maitreya, the Buddha of the future. This figure, 93.5 centimetres high, is one of two great gilt-bronze examples in the National Museum of Korea. The body is slender, the bare torso smooth and the face wears a gentle smile under a low triple crown. Thin walls and a near-perfect casting show advanced technique. Whether it was made in Silla or Baekje is debated. A very similar wooden statue in Kōryū-ji in Kyoto, Japan's first National Treasure in sculpture, is thought by many to be Korean work or closely based on it.
image_file: Gilt-bronze Maitreya in Meditation (National Treasure No. 83) 금동미륵보살반가사유상 (국보 제83호) 02.jpg
image_caption: Pensive Bodhisattva, National Treasure No. 83, National Museum of Korea

title: Shaka Triad of Hōryū-ji
creator: nara-buddhist-workshops
type: Gilt bronze
note: A bronze Buddha with two attendants, signed by Tori Busshi and dedicated after the death of Prince Shōtoku.
description: An inscription on the back of the halo records that the triad was made in 623 by the sculptor Tori, of the Kuratsukuri clan of immigrant saddle-makers, in prayer for Prince Shōtoku, the great early patron of Japanese Buddhism, who died in 622. The historical Buddha Shaka sits cross-legged with hands raised in gestures of reassurance and gift-giving, flanked by two bodhisattvas, all set against a flame-patterned halo. The frontal, symmetrical design, archaic smile and cascading drapery follow Chinese Northern Wei models as transmitted through Korea. Hōryū-ji is among the oldest wooden buildings in the world, and the triad is one of the earliest dated works of Japanese sculpture and a National Treasure.
image_file: Horyuji Shaka Triad.jpg
image_caption: Shaka Triad by Tori Busshi, Hōryū-ji

title: Great Buddha (Daibutsu) of Tōdai-ji
creator: nara-buddhist-workshops
type: Cast bronze, about 15 m
note: The colossal bronze Vairocana of Nara, the largest bronze Buddha in the world when cast, symbol of the Buddhist state of Emperor Shōmu.
description: In 743 Emperor Shōmu issued an edict calling for a giant image of the cosmic Buddha Vairocana (Rushana) to protect the country, as head of a network of provincial temples. Casting took place in several stages between 747 and 749, using huge amounts of copper and gold from across Japan, and the eyes were painted in an eye-opening ceremony in 752 attended by monks from India and China. The statue has been damaged by earthquakes and fires, notably in 1180 and 1567, and the head and much of the body date from repairs in the Edo period; only parts of the base and lotus petals, with engraved images of the Buddhist universe, are original. The present hall, rebuilt in 1709, is still one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.
image_file: Daibutsu Grand bouddha - Tōdai-ji - Nara.jpg
image_caption: The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji

title: Ashura
creator: nara-buddhist-workshops
type: Hollow dry lacquer, painted
note: A slender, three-faced and six-armed Buddhist guardian whose melancholy young faces have made it one of Japan's most loved statues.
description: In 734 Empress Kōmyō commissioned a set of statues for the Western Golden Hall of Kōfuku-ji, the family temple of the Fujiwara, in memory of her mother. They included the Eight Legions, protectors of Buddhism originally drawn from Indian gods and demons. Ashura, in India a warlike demon, is shown as a thin boy with three faces and six arms, wearing only a scarf and skirt. The statue was made in hollow dry lacquer: layers of lacquer-soaked hemp cloth were built up over a clay core, which was then removed, giving a light figure with sensitive modelling. The faces express a gentle sorrow rather than fury, perhaps reflecting repentance. The statue survived the temple's fires and is a National Treasure.
image_file: Kofukuji Ashura 1.jpg
image_caption: Ashura, Kōfuku-ji

title: Seokguram Buddha
creator: korean-buddhist-sculptors
type: Granite
note: A serene granite Buddha in an artificial cave temple on Mount Toham, the masterpiece of Unified Silla art.
description: According to the Samguk yusa, the minister Kim Daeseong began building Seokguram and the nearby temple Bulguksa in 751. Because the local granite was too hard to carve into caves, the builders constructed an artificial grotto of granite blocks covered with earth, with a rectangular antechamber and a round domed rotunda. The seated Buddha, about 3.5 metres high, sits facing east towards the sea, his right hand touching the earth, surrounded by reliefs of bodhisattvas, disciples and guardians. The figure combines volume, calm and precise proportion. Restored, sometimes badly, in the early twentieth century, the grotto is now sealed behind glass. With Bulguksa it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Front view of Seokguram from front chamber.jpg
image_caption: The Buddha of Seokguram seen from the antechamber

title: Amida Nyorai of the Phoenix Hall, Byōdō-in
creator: jocho
type: Gilded wood, joined-block technique
note: The only surviving work by Jōchō: a gilded Amida Buddha in the Phoenix Hall, built as an image of the Western Paradise.
description: In 1052 the regent Fujiwara no Yorimichi turned his villa at Uji into the temple Byōdō-in, and the next year dedicated the Phoenix Hall, whose wings and reflection in a pond were meant to evoke Amida's palace in the Pure Land. Inside sits the Amida Buddha by Jōchō, nearly three metres high, made of joined blocks of cypress wood, covered in lacquer and gold leaf. His calm round face, shallow-carved robes and relaxed posture express the promise of salvation that made Pure Land devotion popular in an age that believed the world was in decline. Above him on the walls fly fifty-two small wooden bodhisattvas playing instruments and dancing on clouds. The hall appears on the Japanese ten-yen coin.
image_file: Byodoin Amitaabha Buddha.JPG
image_caption: Jōchō, Amida Nyorai, Phoenix Hall, Byōdō-in

title: Kongō Rikishi (Niō) of the Great South Gate, Tōdai-ji
creator: unkei
type: Joined wood, about 8.4 m
note: Two colossal guardian kings carved in about seventy days by Unkei, Kaikei and their workshop for the rebuilt Tōdai-ji.
description: After Tōdai-ji was burned in 1180 during the Genpei War, its rebuilding was led by the monk Chōgen. In 1203 the Kei school sculptors carved two guardians for the new Great South Gate: the open-mouthed Agyō and the closed-mouthed Ungyō, representing the first and last sounds of the Sanskrit alphabet. Each is about 8.4 metres tall and built from about three thousand pieces of wood. Inscriptions found during restoration in 1988–93 confirmed that Unkei and Kaikei directed the work with about twenty assistants. The swelling muscles, flying draperies and fierce faces, made to be seen from below, are the most dramatic expression of Kamakura realism. Both figures are National Treasures.
image_file: Nio guardians by Unkei in Nara.jpg
image_caption: Niō guardian at the Great South Gate of Tōdai-ji

title: Muchaku (Asanga)
creator: unkei
type: Painted wood with inlaid crystal eyes
note: A portrait statue of an Indian Buddhist philosopher, carved under Unkei, which seems to show a living, thoughtful old man.
description: Asanga, called Muchaku in Japanese, and his brother Vasubandhu (Seshin) were fourth-century Indian monks who founded the Yogācāra school, important to the Hossō sect of Kōfuku-ji. Their statues were made for the rebuilt Northern Octagonal Hall around 1212, at the end of Unkei's career, and carved by his sons and workshop under his direction. Muchaku, nearly two metres high, stands holding a wrapped cloth bundle, his head slightly bowed, his face lined and inward-looking, with crystal eyes that catch the light. Although no likeness of Asanga existed, the statue has the presence of a portrait of a real person. It is often considered the summit of Japanese portrait sculpture and is a National Treasure.
image_file: Kofukuji Hokuendo Muchaku Unkei.jpg
image_caption: Unkei and workshop, Muchaku, Kōfuku-ji

title: Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy (Bunian tu)
creator: yan-liben
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A record of the Tang emperor receiving the Tibetan envoy who came to escort Princess Wencheng to Tibet in 641.
description: In 640 the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo sent his minister Gar Tongtsen to the Tang court to ask for a princess in marriage, and in 641 Princess Wencheng travelled to Lhasa. The painting shows Emperor Taizong seated on a litter carried by court women, some holding fans and a parasol, and on the left a court official in red, the envoy in a patterned robe and an interpreter. The emperor is much larger than everyone else, following the convention of hierarchic scale, while the women are more slender than in later Tang taste. The painting, traditionally attributed to Yan Liben, is probably a Song copy. It is a key document of Tang court painting and of relations with Tibet.
image_file: Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy(Bunian Tu).jpg
image_caption: Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy, Palace Museum, Beijing

title: Thirteen Emperors Scroll
creator: yan-liben
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: Portraits of thirteen emperors from the Han to the Sui, each with attendants, attributed to Yan Liben.
description: This long scroll presents thirteen rulers from the Western Han to the Sui dynasty, each standing or seated with attendants and identified by an inscription. The emperors are idealised types rather than true likenesses, and they are characterised morally: founders of dynasties appear powerful and dignified, while weak or wicked rulers look feeble. The scroll thus served as a kind of political lesson. Scholars believe the first part is a later replacement and debate how much of the rest is Yan Liben's own work. It entered the Boston museum in 1931 and is one of the most important early Chinese paintings outside China.
image_file: Yan Liben. Thirteen Emperors. Boston, Museum of the Fine Arts.jpg
image_caption: Thirteen Emperors Scroll (detail), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

title: Night-Shining White
creator: han-gan
type: Handscroll, ink on paper
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
note: A portrait of Emperor Xuanzong's favourite horse, rearing against a hitching post, covered with seals and inscriptions of later collectors.
description: Emperor Xuanzong loved horses, and his stables held thousands of fine mounts brought from Central Asia. Night-Shining White (Zhaoye bai) was one of his favourite chargers. Han Gan shows it tied to a post, tossing its head with flaring nostrils and rolling eyes, its body powerfully rounded and modelled with light ink washes; the tail and part of the legs were retouched later. Over the centuries collectors, including the Southern Tang ruler Li Yu and the Qianlong Emperor, added seals and inscriptions, so that the picture is surrounded by a record of its ownership. The painting passed through several Western collections before entering the Metropolitan Museum in 1977.
image_file: Night Shining White 唐 韓幹 照夜白圖 卷.jpg
image_caption: Han Gan, Night-Shining White, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Eighty-seven Celestials
creator: wu-daozi
type: Handscroll, ink on silk
note: A procession of Daoist deities in flowing robes, drawn in pure ink outline, sometimes attributed to Wu Daozi.
description: This unpainted scroll, nearly three metres long, shows a procession of eighty-seven Daoist immortals and attendants crossing a bridge and walking past railings, carrying banners, flowers and instruments. It is drawn entirely in ink line (baimiao) with rhythmic, flowing strokes that suggest a draft for a temple mural. The painter Xu Beihong bought it in Hong Kong in 1937 and attributed it to Wu Daozi, though many scholars date it to the Song and connect it with the eleventh-century painter Wu Zongyuan. It was briefly stolen during the war with Japan and later recovered. Whatever its author, it is the best surviving example of the Tang-style figure line associated with Wu's school.
image_file: Eighty-seven Celestials.jpg
image_caption: Eighty-seven Celestials (detail)

title: Sancai camel carrying musicians
creator: tang-sancai-potters
type: Glazed earthenware tomb figure
note: A Bactrian camel bearing a band of Central Asian musicians and a dancer, found in a Tang tomb at Xi'an.
description: This figure, about 58 centimetres high, was excavated in 1957 from the tomb of Xianyu Tinghui, a general who died in 723, in the western suburbs of Xi'an. A two-humped camel stands with its head thrown back, carrying on a rug-covered platform seven musicians playing lutes, flutes and pipes, mostly bearded foreigners, and a dancer in the middle. The camel and the figures were moulded separately, painted with amber, green and cream glazes that run together, and fired at a low temperature. It shows the Silk Road world of the Tang capital, where Central Asian music and dance were highly fashionable. It is one of the masterpieces of sancai and of Tang tomb sculpture.
image_file: Sancai-glazed foreign musicians on camel. 723 CE.jpg
image_caption: Sancai camel with musicians, 723, National Museum of China

title: Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew (Jizhi wengao)
creator: yan-zhenqing
type: Calligraphy, ink on paper, handscroll
note: Yan Zhenqing's grief-stricken draft eulogy for a nephew killed in the An Lushan rebellion, prized as the second-greatest running script after the Orchid Pavilion.
description: In 756, during the An Lushan rebellion, Yan Zhenqing's cousin Yan Gaoqing and his son Yan Jiming were captured and killed when their city fell after a heroic defence. Two years later Yan Zhenqing recovered his nephew's head and wrote this eulogy. It is a draft, with words crossed out and inserted, and the writing changes as he goes, from controlled characters to rushing, slanting lines as his anger and grief grow. Later critics valued it precisely because it was not meant as a work of art and so shows feeling directly. Collectors and emperors added seals and colophons, and since the eighteenth century it has often been called the second greatest running-script work in China.
image_file: Yan Zhenqing - Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew.jpg
image_caption: Yan Zhenqing, Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew

title: Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk
creator: huizong
year: early 12th century, after Zhang Xuan (8th century)
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A copy, traditionally attributed to Emperor Huizong, of a lost Tang painting of court women beating, ironing and sewing silk.
description: The Tang painter Zhang Xuan, active in the court of Xuanzong in the eighth century, was famous for scenes of palace women. His painting of women preparing silk is lost, but this copy, with an inscription in Huizong's hand, preserves the composition. In three groups, the women pound silk with long pestles, sew and stretch out a length of cloth to be ironed with a pan of hot coals, while a little girl plays underneath. The full-figured women, bright colours and patterned clothes reflect Tang taste; the copy was probably made by Huizong's academy painters. It entered the Boston museum in 1912 and is a key document of Tang figure painting.
image_file: Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk.jpg
image_caption: Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

title: The Night Revels of Han Xizai
creator: gu-hongzhong
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A five-part scene of an official's evening of music, dancing and entertainment, said to have been painted as a report to his ruler.
description: The scroll is divided by screens into five scenes: Han Xizai and his guests listening to a pipa player, watching a dancer while Han beats a drum, resting on a couch, listening to flutes, and saying goodbye to guests. Han appears several times, always unsmiling, with his tall hat, and the painter records furniture, musical instruments, costumes and food in exact detail. According to tradition, the Southern Tang ruler Li Yu sent Gu Hongzhong to observe Han's parties because he was considering him for high office, and Han, sensing the danger of politics, deliberately behaved badly. The work is now generally regarded as a later copy. It is a masterpiece of Chinese figure painting.
image_file: Gu Hongzhong's Night Revels 1 edit (cropped2) (cropped) (cropped).jpg
image_caption: The Night Revels of Han Xizai (detail)

title: Travellers among Mountains and Streams
creator: fan-kuan
type: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on silk
note: A towering mountain rising above a tiny mule train, the defining image of Northern Song monumental landscape.
description: Nearly two metres high, the painting is divided into three planes: boulders in the foreground, a wooded hill with a temple roof and a mule train of travellers in the middle, and in the back a vast cliff, with a thin waterfall at its right, filling most of the picture. A band of mist separates the mountain from the foreground, so that it seems both near and immeasurably far. Fan Kuan built the rock faces with thousands of short texture strokes, called raindrop strokes, that give a sense of solid, gritty stone. The travellers are almost invisible, stressing the smallness of humans in the order of nature. The painting was long attributed to him, and in 1958 his signature was found hidden among the leaves. It has inspired painters for nearly a thousand years.
image_file: Fan Kuan - Travelers Among Mountains and Streams - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: Fan Kuan, Travellers among Mountains and Streams

title: Early Spring
creator: guo-xi
type: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on silk
note: A mountain dissolving in spring mist, dated 1072, which puts into practice Guo Xi's theories of landscape painting.
description: Signed and dated in the year 1072, Early Spring was painted while Guo Xi was court painter to Emperor Shenzong. A central mountain rises in an S-curve, built of swelling forms that seem to move, with twisting, claw-like trees, waterfalls, pavilions and small figures of fishermen and travellers. Guo Xi uses shifting viewpoints, the high, deep and level distances described in his treatise, so the eye can wander from the foreground to the summit. Washes of mist suggest the moist air of early spring and the awakening of nature. The painting is one of the few securely dated Northern Song masterpieces and a classic of Chinese landscape.
image_file: Guo Xi - Early Spring (large).jpg
image_caption: Guo Xi, Early Spring, 1072

title: Whispering Pines in the Mountains
creator: li-tang
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A monumental landscape signed by Li Tang and dated 1124, painted just before the fall of the Northern Song.
description: A tall central peak rises behind a group of tall pine trees, with a waterfall, a stream and a small figure seated by the water. Li Tang's signature and the date are written on the distant peak. The painting still follows the monumental tradition of Fan Kuan, but the rocks are modelled with broader, blockier axe-cut strokes and the composition is more compact. Three years later Kaifeng fell to the Jurchen and Li Tang fled south, where his style evolved further, so this work is an important document of the transition from Northern to Southern Song painting.
image_file: Li Tang - Wind in Pines Among a Myriad Valleys.jpg
image_caption: Li Tang, Whispering Pines in the Mountains, 1124

title: Auspicious Cranes
creator: huizong
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: Twenty cranes circling over the palace gate of Kaifeng, painted to record an auspicious event in 1112.
description: According to the accompanying text written in Huizong's slender-gold script, on the evening of the Lantern Festival in 1112 a flock of cranes appeared over the Xuande Gate of the palace in Kaifeng, circling and calling, and two landed on the roof. The emperor took this as a sign of heaven's favour and recorded it in painting and poem. Against a blue sky of mineral pigment the white cranes, each in a different position, fly over the ridge of the roof, painted from directly in front. Such paintings of auspicious omens were part of Huizong's efforts to legitimise his reign; fifteen years later the dynasty lost the north. It is one of the most beautiful works associated with him.
image_file: Auspicious Cranes.jpg
image_caption: Auspicious Cranes, Liaoning Provincial Museum

title: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
creator: zhang-zeduan
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A five-metre panorama of a Song city and its river traffic, crowded with more than 800 figures.
description: Unrolled from right to left, the scroll moves from quiet countryside with farmhouses and willows, along the river with heavily loaded barges, to the climax at a great rainbow bridge where a boat is about to collide with it and crowds watch from above, and then through a city gate into busy streets of shops, inns and temples. Zhang Zeduan recorded carts, boats and buildings with the precision of ruled-line painting, and people at every kind of activity. It is usually thought to show the Northern Song capital Kaifeng, though the exact festival and place are debated. The scroll was copied and reworked many times, and the Qing court version by five painters is also famous. Its rare displays in Beijing draw huge queues.
image_file: Bianjing city gate.JPG
image_caption: Along the River During the Qingming Festival (detail of the city gate)

title: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains
creator: wang-ximeng
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A nearly 12-metre blue-and-green panorama of lakes and mountains painted by an eighteen-year-old student of Emperor Huizong.
description: The scroll is about 12 metres long and shows a vast landscape of mountains, lakes, rivers and bridges, with villages, temples, mills, fishermen and travellers. It is painted in the blue-and-green style, with layers of azurite and malachite over ink and ochre, an archaic manner associated with the Tang. According to the colophon by Cai Jing, Huizong personally guided the young Wang Ximeng, who finished the work in half a year in 1113 and died soon after. The brilliant mineral colours have survived remarkably well. The painting is one of the most celebrated in Chinese art and has inspired modern dance and films.
image_file: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains part.jpg
image_caption: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains (section)

title: Walking on a Mountain Path in Spring
creator: ma-yuan
type: Album leaf, ink and colour on silk
note: A scholar strolls under willows while a bird takes flight, a small album leaf in Ma Yuan's one-corner style, with a couplet by Emperor Ningzong.
description: In the lower left corner a scholar in a long robe walks along a path with a servant carrying a qin zither, brushing against willow branches. Two birds perch and one flies away into empty space. The rest of the leaf is almost bare silk, suggesting misty spring air. On the right are two lines of poetry written by Emperor Ningzong, saying that the wild flowers dance when the sleeves brush past them and the hidden birds do not sing at the sight of people. The composition shows how Ma Yuan concentrated forms in one corner to create a poetic mood, and the union of image and court poetry typical of Southern Song academy painting.
image_file: Ma Yuan Walking on Path in Spring.jpg
image_caption: Ma Yuan, Walking on a Mountain Path in Spring

title: Water (twelve album leaves)
creator: ma-yuan
type: Twelve leaves mounted as a handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: Twelve studies of water in different moods, from gentle ripples to stormy waves, painted entirely in line.
description: Each of the twelve leaves shows water in a different condition, with a title written by Empress Yang: waves on the Yellow River, autumn waters of Dongting Lake, clouds rising from the green sea, layered waves, a gentle breeze on a lake. Apart from a little land in one or two leaves, they are made almost only of ink lines, thick and thin, curling, breaking and repeating, that suggest movement and texture. The series is a virtuoso display of brushwork and close observation of nature. It is one of the few works by Ma Yuan that do not include figures, and shows how far Song painters could push a single subject.
image_file: Ma Yuan - Water Album - Clouds Rising from the Green Sea.jpg
image_caption: Ma Yuan, Clouds Rising from the Green Sea, from the Water album

title: Pure and Remote Views of Streams and Mountains
creator: xia-gui
type: Handscroll, ink on paper
note: A nine-metre ink handscroll of rivers, rocks and villages that reveals Xia Gui's bold, abbreviated brushwork.
description: The scroll unfolds as a journey: rocky cliffs, a river with boats, a village, a bridge, mountains half lost in mist, and travellers on paths. Xia Gui used only ink on paper, with strong, angular axe-cut strokes for the rocks and wet, splashed washes for the distance, alternating dense passages with open space. The work has the rhythm of a piece of music, with crescendos and pauses. It shows the dramatic, compressed style of the Southern Song academy at its most powerful and was a model for Japanese ink painters such as Sesshū.
image_file: Xia Gui, Streams and Mountains with a Clear Distant View, detail.jpg
image_caption: Xia Gui, Pure and Remote Views of Streams and Mountains (detail)

title: Six Persimmons
creator: mu-qi
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: Six persimmons in a row, painted in different tones of ink, a famous example of Chan simplicity.
description: Six persimmons sit in a line on an empty ground, some outlined, some filled with dark or pale ink, their stems painted with quick strokes. Nothing else is shown. The painting is traditionally attributed to Muqi, though it is not signed and the attribution is debated. It was brought to Japan and kept in the Zen temple Daitoku-ji in Kyoto, where it is shown only rarely. In the twentieth century it became celebrated in the West as an emblem of Zen Buddhism, its plainness and balance seen as expressing emptiness and the suchness of things. Whatever its meaning, it shows a remarkable control of ink tone.
image_file: 六柿图.jpg
image_caption: Six Persimmons, attributed to Muqi, Daitoku-ji

title: Immortal in Splashed Ink
creator: liang-kai
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: A pot-bellied immortal painted with a few broad, wet strokes, an early masterpiece of abbreviated brush painting.
description: A plump, bald figure with drooping eyebrows shuffles forward, his robe painted with a handful of sweeping, wet strokes and his face with a few touches of fine line. The figure, perhaps a Daoist immortal or an eccentric, seems both comic and wise. The method, called splashed ink or abbreviated brush, relied on speed and confidence and was linked with Chan Buddhist ideas of sudden enlightenment. Liang Kai had left the court academy, and his free work was little appreciated by Chinese critics but highly valued in Japan, where this scroll is a National Treasure.
image_file: Liang Kai - Immortal in Splashed Ink.jpg
image_caption: Liang Kai, Immortal in Splashed Ink, Tokyo National Museum

title: Cold Food Observance (Hanshi tie)
creator: su-shi
type: Calligraphy, ink on paper, handscroll
note: Two poems written by Su Shi in exile at Huangzhou, ranked among the three greatest works of running script.
description: In 1082, three years into his banishment at Huangzhou, Su Shi wrote two poems on the Cold Food festival, when fires are put out before the Qingming festival. They describe the rain, his poor hut, his cold kitchen, and his despair at being far from the capital and his ancestors' graves. In the writing the characters grow larger and heavier as the emotion intensifies, with some strokes stretched out dramatically. The poet Huang Tingjian added a colophon praising it. The scroll, scorched when the Yuanmingyuan was burned in 1860, was in Japan for some decades before returning to China. It is often called the third greatest work of running script, after Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion and Yan Zhenqing's Requiem to My Nephew.
image_file: Su Shi-Cold Food Observance.jpg
image_caption: Su Shi, Cold Food Observance

title: Ru ware narcissus basin
creator: song-potters
type: Stoneware with celadon glaze
note: An oval basin of the rare Ru ware made for the Northern Song court, with a soft blue-green glaze and fine crackle.
description: The Ru kilns at Qingliangsi in Baofeng, Henan, made ceramics for the court of the Northern Song for only a few decades around 1100, and fewer than a hundred pieces are known. Their glaze, which is said to contain powdered agate, is an opaque, soft bluish green like a sky after rain, with a fine network of crackle; the pieces were fired on tiny spurs, leaving small sesame-seed marks on the base. This oval basin, without any crackle, is one of the most perfect examples. It was later called a narcissus basin, though it was probably made for another use. The Qianlong Emperor had a poem incised on its base and a stand made for it. Ru ware set the ideal of quiet monochrome elegance for later Chinese ceramics.
image_file: 北宋汝窯青瓷無紋水仙盆 含底座.tif
image_caption: Ru ware narcissus basin, National Palace Museum, Taipei

title: Jian ware tea bowl with hare's-fur glaze
creator: song-potters
type: Stoneware with iron-rich glaze
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (many examples worldwide)
note: A dark tea bowl from the Jian kilns of Fujian, whose streaked glaze set off the white froth of whisked tea; called tenmoku in Japan.
description: In Song China tea was made by whisking powdered leaves in hot water to a white froth, and tea contests judged how long the froth lasted. Dark bowls from the Jian kilns in Fujian showed it off best. Their thick iron-rich glaze breaks into fine brown and silvery streaks known as hare's fur, or, in rare cases, oil spots or iridescent rainbow spots. The emperor Huizong praised these bowls in his treatise on tea. Japanese monks studying at Zen monasteries on Mount Tianmu brought them home, and in Japan they were called tenmoku and became treasured utensils of the tea ceremony. Three iridescent yōhen tenmoku bowls in Japanese collections are National Treasures.
image_file: 中國 南宋 建窯 兔毫釉茶碗-Tea Bowl with “Hare’s-Fur” Glaze MET DP372022.jpg
image_caption: Jian ware tea bowl with hare's-fur glaze, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Goryeo celadon maebyeong with inlaid cranes and clouds
creator: goryeo-celadon-potters
type: Stoneware with inlaid decoration under celadon glaze
note: A tall Korean celadon vase inlaid with flying cranes in roundels, the most famous example of the sanggam technique.
description: The maebyeong, a vase with broad shoulders and a small mouth, was used for wine or decoratively for a branch of plum blossom. This example, about 42 centimetres high, is covered with sixty-nine cranes, some flying up within circular medallions and some flying down between them, among clouds. The designs were incised into the clay and filled with white and black slip before glazing and firing, the inlay technique called sanggam that Goryeo potters perfected. The cranes, symbols of longevity, seem to float in the soft blue-green glaze. The collector Jeon Hyeong-pil bought the vase in 1935 to keep it in Korea, paying a famous sum; it is now National Treasure No. 68.
image_file: 청자 상감 구름 학 무늬 매병 고려-靑磁象嵌雲鶴文梅甁 高麗-Maebyeong decorated with cranes and clouds MET DP240197.jpg
image_caption: A similar Goryeo maebyeong with inlaid cranes and clouds, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Celadon incense burner with openwork lid
creator: goryeo-celadon-potters
type: Stoneware with celadon glaze
note: An incense burner with an openwork globe lid supported by three rabbits, a virtuoso example of plain Goryeo celadon.
description: This incense burner, National Treasure No. 95, is composed of three parts: a lid formed as an openwork sphere of interlocking circles, through which the smoke escapes; a bowl shaped like a lotus flower, decorated with inlaid details; and a base supported by three small crouching rabbits. Its pure kingfisher-coloured glaze is the kind described by the Chinese envoy Xu Jing in 1123. Combining modelling, openwork, inlay and white slip details, it shows the technical range of Goryeo potters at the height of their art in the twelfth century, before the inlaid wares became dominant.
image_file: Korea - Seoul - National Museum - Incense Burner 0252-06a.jpg
image_caption: Goryeo celadon incense burner, National Museum of Korea

title: Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara
creator: goryeo-buddhist-painters
type: Hanging scroll, ink, colour and gold on silk
location: Kagami Shrine, Karatsu (on deposit at Saga Prefectural Museum), and other collections in Japan and Korea
note: A Goryeo Buddhist painting of the bodhisattva of compassion seated on a rock by the water, veiled in transparent gauze.
description: Goryeo Buddhist paintings, made mainly in the fourteenth century for the court and aristocracy, are among the most luxurious of East Asian religious images, and about 160 survive, most of them in Japan. The Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara shows the bodhisattva seated on a rocky ledge by the sea on Mount Potalaka, with a willow branch in a vase, bamboo behind, and the pilgrim boy Sudhana below asking for guidance. The figure wears a translucent white veil painted over brilliant red, green and gold, and the patterns are painted in gold line with extraordinary finesse. The paintings were made by professional painters, sometimes named in inscriptions, such as Seo Gubang. They express the devout luxury of the late Goryeo elite.
image_file: Goryeo-Avalokiteshvara-1310-kagami Jinjya Temple.jpg
image_caption: Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara, 1310, Kagami Shrine, Karatsu

title: Autumn Colors on the Qiao and Hua Mountains
creator: zhao-mengfu
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on paper
note: A landscape painted for a friend who had never seen his family's home province, a turning point for Yuan literati painting.
description: Zhao Mengfu painted this short scroll after returning from service in the north, for his friend Zhou Mi, whose family came from Shandong but who had never been there. It shows two mountains near Jinan, the pointed Mount Hua and the rounded Mount Qiao, across a flat marshy plain with trees, houses, fishermen and goats. The style deliberately looks back to Tang and Five Dynasties painters such as Dong Yuan, with simple forms, archaic perspective and restrained colour, rather than to the dramatic manner of the Southern Song. It embodies Zhao's idea of the spirit of antiquity and opened the way for the Four Yuan Masters. The Qianlong Emperor added several inscriptions.
image_file: 2 Zhao Mengfu Autumn Colors on the Qiao and Hua Mountains Handscroll, ink and colors on paper, 28.4 x 93.2 cm National Palace Museum, Taipei..jpg
image_caption: Zhao Mengfu, Autumn Colors on the Qiao and Hua Mountains

title: Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains
creator: huang-gongwang
type: Handscroll, ink on paper
location: National Palace Museum, Taipei, and Zhejiang Provincial Museum, Hangzhou
note: Huang Gongwang's masterpiece, a long river landscape that was burned in two and is divided between Taipei and Hangzhou.
description: Huang Gongwang painted this scroll for a Daoist friend, Wuyong, over three or four years, adding to it whenever he had time. It shows the scenery of the Fuchun River near Hangzhou: gently rolling hills, trees, villages and fishing boats, built up with dry, layered hemp-fibre strokes and pale ink, an image of quiet seclusion rather than grandeur. In 1650 its owner, Wu Hongyu, ordered it to be burned as he was dying so that it would go with him, but his nephew pulled it from the fire. The small first section, The Remaining Mountain, is in Hangzhou, the longer part in Taipei. The Qianlong Emperor wrote many inscriptions on what turned out to be a copy, and he dismissed the genuine one. The two parts were shown together in Taipei in 2011.
image_file: Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains (first half).JPG
image_caption: Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains (part)

title: The Rongxi Studio
creator: ni-zan
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: A near riverbank with thin trees and an empty pavilion, wide water and distant hills: Ni Zan's classic spare composition.
description: In the foreground a few slender trees rise from rocks beside an empty thatched pavilion; across a wide expanse of blank paper, representing water, are low distant hills. The ink is pale and dry, applied with a slanted brush in sideways strokes. Ni Zan painted it for a physician called Rengzhong, adding a poem describing it as the studio of his friend; the name, Rongxi Studio, means a studio just big enough to fit one's knees, an image of contentment with little. The absence of people and the restraint of the composition expressed for later scholars the purity and detachment of the recluse. The painting is one of his most famous and was much copied.
image_file: Ni Zan. The Rongxi Studio.1372. 74,7x35,3. National Palace Museum, Taipei.jpg
image_caption: Ni Zan, The Rongxi Studio, 1372

title: Dwelling in the Qingbian Mountains
creator: wang-meng
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: A densely packed mountain landscape full of restless, twisting forms, which Dong Qichang called the finest painting in the world.
description: The Qingbian (Bian) mountains near Wang Meng's home of Huzhou were the site of the retreat of his cousin, and in 1366, as the Yuan dynasty was collapsing in war, he painted this tall landscape. Mountains rise in writhing, rippling masses to the top of the paper, covered with ox-hair and unravelled-rope texture strokes and thick dots of vegetation; a tiny scholar sits in a hut in a fold of the hills. The crowding and agitation of the forms have been read as expressing the anxiety of the times. Dong Qichang praised it in an inscription in 1616. It is one of the masterpieces of Yuan painting.
image_file: Wang Meng Dwelling in the Qingbian Mountains. ink on paper. 1366. 141x42,2 cm. Shanghai Museum.jpg
image_caption: Wang Meng, Dwelling in the Qingbian Mountains, 1366

title: The David Vases
creator: jingdezhen-potters
type: Porcelain with underglaze cobalt-blue decoration
note: A pair of temple vases dated 1351, the most important early blue-and-white porcelain, named after the collector Sir Percival David.
description: These two tall vases, each about 63 centimetres high, are painted in underglaze cobalt blue with dragons among clouds, phoenixes, lotus and plantain leaves, and have handles shaped like elephant heads. An inscription on the neck states that a man named Zhang Wenjin donated them with an incense burner to a Daoist temple in Jiangxi in 1351, wishing for the protection and prosperity of his family. Because they are dated, they proved that sophisticated blue-and-white porcelain was being made at Jingdezhen during the Yuan dynasty, earlier than once thought. The vases were bought separately in the 1920s and 30s by Sir Percival David and reunited; his collection is now displayed at the British Museum.
image_file: The David Vases.jpg
image_caption: The David Vases, British Museum

title: Illustrated Handscrolls of The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari emaki)
creator: yamato-e-painters
type: Handscroll sections, ink and colour on paper
location: Tokugawa Art Museum, Nagoya, and Gotoh Museum, Tokyo
note: The oldest surviving illustrations of Murasaki Shikibu's novel, the masterpiece of Heian court painting.
description: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji in the early eleventh century, and about a hundred years later the court produced lavish illustrated scrolls of it, perhaps for an imperial or Fujiwara patron. Of an original set of perhaps twenty scrolls, about twenty pictures and accompanying passages of calligraphy on decorated paper survive. The pictures use the conventions of tsukuri-e, built-up colour, with roofless interiors seen from above, steep diagonals, and stylised faces with slit eyes and hooked noses that leave emotion to posture and setting. Scenes such as Genji holding the baby Kaoru, who is not his son, express hidden sorrow with remarkable restraint. The scrolls are National Treasures, and the paintings were restored and reconstructed digitally in the 2000s.
image_file: Genji emaki Yadorigi.JPG
image_caption: Yadorigi scene from the Genji scrolls, Tokugawa Art Museum

title: Frolicking Animals (Chōjū-jinbutsu-giga)
creator: yamato-e-painters
type: Four handscrolls, ink on paper
location: Kōzan-ji, Kyoto (on deposit at Tokyo and Kyoto National Museums)
note: Four ink scrolls of rabbits, frogs and monkeys playing at being humans, often called the oldest Japanese manga.
description: The four scrolls preserved at the temple Kōzan-ji were painted by different hands over perhaps a century. The first and most famous shows rabbits, frogs and monkeys bathing, wrestling, holding archery contests and conducting a Buddhist service, in which a frog sits as the Buddha before a monkey monk. The second shows real and imaginary animals, the third and fourth people and animals at games. The scrolls use only ink line, drawn with lively speed, and have no text, so their satirical meaning is uncertain. They are traditionally attributed to the abbot Toba Sōjō, but this is unproven. Their humour and storytelling have made them famous as a forerunner of manga.
image_file: Chouju sumo2.jpg
image_caption: Rabbit and frog wrestling, first scroll of the Chōjū-giga

title: Legends of Mount Shigi (Shigisan engi emaki)
creator: yamato-e-painters
type: Three handscrolls, ink and colour on paper
location: Chōgosonshi-ji, Nara (on deposit at Nara National Museum)
note: Three scrolls telling the miracles of the monk Myōren, including a flying rice bowl that carries away a rich man's storehouse.
description: The scrolls tell stories of Myōren, a monk who lived on Mount Shigi near Nara in the tenth century. In the first, the 'flying granary', his begging bowl flies down to a rich man's house and, when the man refuses to fill it, lifts his whole storehouse and carries it to the mountain, while the household runs after it in panic. Other scrolls show Myōren curing an emperor and his sister's search for him. In contrast to the Genji scrolls, the painting uses lively, flowing line, many small figures with expressive faces and continuous narrative. The work shows how yamato-e handled crowds, movement and humour.
image_file: Sigisanengi tobikura.jpg
image_caption: The flying granary, Shigisan engi

title: Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace (Heiji monogatari emaki)
creator: yamato-e-painters
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on paper
note: A dramatic scroll of warriors burning a palace and abducting a retired emperor during the Heiji Rebellion of 1159.
description: In 1159 the warrior Minamoto no Yoshitomo and the courtier Fujiwara no Nobuyori attacked the Sanjō palace of the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa, carried him off and set the palace on fire. The scroll, about seven metres long, shows the attack as a mounting storm of horses, armour and flame, with soldiers killing courtiers and ladies trying to escape, then the procession of victors leaving. The masses of figures, red flames and swirling smoke give it an extraordinary energy. It belonged to a set of scrolls illustrating the war tale Heiji monogatari, of which parts are in Tokyo. The scroll left Japan in the nineteenth century and is one of the great treasures of the Boston museum.
image_file: Heiji Monogatari Emaki - Sanjo scroll part 5 - v2.jpg
image_caption: Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace (detail), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

title: Catching a Catfish with a Gourd (Hyōnen-zu)
creator: josetsu
type: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on paper
note: A Zen riddle in paint: a man tries to catch a slippery catfish with a smooth gourd, beneath poems by thirty-one monks.
description: The shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi commissioned this painting, originally for a small standing screen, and had thirty-one Zen monks of Kyoto compose verses in answer to the question it poses: how can one catch a catfish with a gourd? A man stands on a riverbank holding a gourd while a catfish swims in the stream, with bamboo and misty mountains around. The riddle, like a kōan, points to the impossibility of grasping the mind through reason. The painting adapts Southern Song ink techniques in a soft, misty manner and is the founding work of Muromachi ink painting. It is a National Treasure.
image_file: Hyônen zu by Josetsu.jpg
image_caption: Josetsu, Catching a Catfish with a Gourd

title: Autumn and Winter Landscapes
creator: sesshu
type: Pair of hanging scrolls, ink on paper
note: Two small ink landscapes whose winter scene, cut through by a jagged vertical line, shows Sesshū's forceful, structured style.
description: Each scroll is less than fifty centimetres high. In the autumn landscape a path winds past a temple and trees towards distant peaks; in the winter landscape a traveller climbs towards a temple in snow, while behind him a sharp, broken vertical stroke, perhaps the edge of a cliff, splits the sky. The brushwork is hard, angular and dark, and the forms are tightly locked together, quite unlike the misty manner of earlier Japanese ink painting. The pair may once have belonged to a set of the four seasons. Both are National Treasures and among the best-known works of Japanese ink painting.
image_file: Sesshu "Autumn And Winter Landscapes" Winter.jpg
image_caption: Sesshū, Winter Landscape

title: Long Landscape Scroll (Sansui chōkan)
creator: sesshu
type: Handscroll, ink and light colour on paper
note: A sixteen-metre handscroll that travels through the four seasons, painted by Sesshū at sixty-seven for his patrons in Yamaguchi.
description: Sesshū painted this scroll in 1486 at his studio in Yamaguchi, under the patronage of the Ōuchi family, and it later passed to the Mōri lords who succeeded them. It begins with spring hills and moves through summer, autumn and winter, past fishing villages, mountain passes, a walled town and boats, ending in snow. Drawing on the Southern Song and Ming models he had seen in China, Sesshū combined them into a continuous journey with varied brushwork, crisp outlines and pale colour. At about sixteen metres, it is his longest work and a summary of his art. It is a National Treasure.
image_file: Landscapes of the Four Seasons by Sesshu (Mori Museum).jpg
image_caption: Sesshū, Long Landscape Scroll (section), Mōri Museum

title: Splashed-Ink Landscape (Haboku sansui)
creator: sesshu
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: A landscape made of a few wet splashes of ink, painted by Sesshū for a departing pupil, with his own account of his life.
description: In 1495 Sesshū's pupil Sōen was about to return to Kamakura, and the old master painted this landscape as a certificate of his training. A few broad, wet strokes suggest a hill, trees, a tavern flag and boat, dissolving into mist. Above, Sesshū wrote a long inscription recalling his journey to China and his teachers Josetsu and Shūbun, followed by poems by six Zen monks. The splashed-ink technique, associated with the Chinese painter Yujian, depends on rapid, controlled accident. The painting is a National Treasure and an important document of Sesshū's view of his own lineage.
image_file: Sesshu - Haboku-Sansui - complete.jpg
image_caption: Sesshū, Splashed-Ink Landscape, 1495

title: Lofty Mount Lu
creator: shen-zhou
type: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on paper
note: A towering landscape painted by Shen Zhou as a birthday gift for his teacher, in the dense manner of Wang Meng.
description: Shen Zhou painted this large scroll, nearly two metres high, to celebrate the seventieth birthday of his teacher Chen Kuan, whose family came from the region of Mount Lu in Jiangxi. Shen had never seen the mountain, and the landscape is an imaginative tribute rather than a view: a great mass of peaks, a waterfall and pines rise above a tiny scholar on the bank. The dense, layered texture strokes are a homage to the Yuan master Wang Meng, while the long poem at the top praises Chen Kuan's character as lofty as the mountain. It is Shen Zhou's most ambitious early work.
image_file: Lofty Mt.Lu by Shen Zhou.jpg
image_caption: Shen Zhou, Lofty Mount Lu, 1467

title: Garden of the Humble Administrator (album)
creator: wen-zhengming
type: Album of thirty-one leaves, ink on paper
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
note: Views of a great Suzhou garden, each paired with a poem, painted by Wen Zhengming for the garden's owner.
description: The Humble Administrator's Garden in Suzhou was created in the early sixteenth century by Wang Xianchen, a retired official, whose name for it alluded to a text about living simply. Wen Zhengming, a friend of the owner, wrote an account of the garden and painted it in an album in 1533, picturing thirty-one sites, pavilions, bridges, ponds, rocks and groves, each with a poem in his calligraphy. The paintings are quiet and spare, showing a scholar at leisure in each setting. The album is both a work of literati art and a record of a garden that, much changed, still survives and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Garden of the Inept Administrator - leaf aa.jpg
image_caption: A leaf from Wen Zhengming's garden album, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Tao Gu Presenting a Poem
creator: tang-yin
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A story of seduction from the tenth century, painted with Tang Yin's refined skill in figures and setting.
description: According to the story, the Song envoy Tao Gu, visiting the Southern Tang court, behaved with great dignity until the courtesan Qin Ruolan, disguised as a post-house servant, seduced him, and he gave her a poem, which was later used to shame him at a banquet. Tang Yin shows Tao Gu sitting in a garden under banana palms, listening as she plays the pipa beside a candle. The figures are painted in fine lines and soft colour, and the setting of rocks and trees is elegant. Tang Yin's own poem on the painting comments ironically on the scene. The work shows his mix of professional skill and literary wit.
image_file: Tao Gu Presents a Poem by Tang Yin.JPG
image_caption: Tang Yin, Tao Gu Presenting a Poem

title: Spring Morning in the Han Palace
creator: qiu-ying
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A long scroll of palace ladies dressing, playing music, painting and tending flowers, the masterpiece of Qiu Ying's fine-line style.
description: Nearly six metres long, the scroll imagines life in the women's quarters of the Han dynasty palace on a spring morning. More than a hundred women and attendants dress, play the qin and pipa, play chess, dance, read, feed peacocks and pose for a portrait painter, an allusion to the story of Wang Zhaojun, who refused to bribe the court painter. The palace buildings, trees and rocks are painted with meticulous ruled lines and brilliant colour. Qiu Ying, a professional painter, made it for a wealthy patron. It was later in the Qing imperial collection and became a model for court painters.
image_file: Qiu Ying Spring morning in the Han palace.jpg
image_caption: Qiu Ying, Spring Morning in the Han Palace (section)

title: The Qingbian Mountains
creator: dong-qichang
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: Dong Qichang's monumental reworking of Dong Yuan and Wang Meng, rearranging mountain forms into near-abstract masses.
description: In this large scroll, painted in 1617, Dong Qichang took up the subject of Wang Meng's famous Dwelling in the Qingbian Mountains, which he had praised, and the style of the tenth-century master Dong Yuan. But he did not copy them: the mountains are built from repeated, clearly outlined blocks that tilt and interlock without a consistent ground plane, and their volumes are flattened into patterns of light and dark. Dong's inscription says that he wished to vie with the old masters. The painting illustrates his idea that a painter should transform rather than imitate the ancients. It is one of the most important Chinese paintings in the West.
image_file: Dong Qichang. The Qingbian Mountains 1617 Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
image_caption: Dong Qichang, The Qingbian Mountains, 1617

title: Ink Grapes
creator: xu-wei
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: A grapevine painted in wild, splashed ink, with Xu Wei's poem lamenting that his pearls of talent are thrown away unsold.
description: A vine hangs down the paper in sweeping, wet strokes, with grapes made of blots of ink in different tones and leaves that blur into each other. Xu Wei wrote a poem at the top, in a rough, tilting hand, saying that he is half his life poor and old, standing alone in his study in the evening wind, and that his bright pearls have nowhere to be sold and are thrown among wild vines. The painting merges calligraphy, poetry and image into a single expression of frustration and genius. It became a model for the freely expressive xieyi style of later painters.
image_file: Xu Wei Grapes.jpg
image_caption: Xu Wei, Ink Grapes

title: Blue-and-white palace bowl with a dragon
creator: jingdezhen-potters
type: Porcelain with underglaze cobalt-blue decoration
location: Palace Museum, Beijing (many in museums worldwide)
note: Imperial Ming blue-and-white of the Xuande reign, painted with a vigorous five-clawed dragon, the classic court porcelain.
description: From the early fifteenth century the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen produced blue-and-white porcelain for the Ming court bearing the reign mark of the emperor, a practice that became standard. The Xuande reign is considered the high point of early Ming blue-and-white, with cobalt from Persia, called sumali, that gives a deep blue with dark spots where the pigment gathered. Dragons with five claws, reserved for the emperor, chase flaming pearls among clouds or waves. The porcelain was used at court and given as gifts to foreign rulers, and similar wares were traded to the Middle East, where collections such as the Ardebil shrine in Iran preserve them. Ming blue-and-white became the most imitated ceramic style in the world, from Vietnam and Persia to Delft.
image_file: Blue and white Ming Xuande 1426 1435.jpg
image_caption: Ming blue-and-white porcelain of the Xuande reign

title: Doucai chicken cup
creator: jingdezhen-potters
type: Porcelain with underglaze blue and overglaze enamels
location: Palace Museum, Beijing; National Palace Museum, Taipei; private collections
note: A tiny wine cup painted with a rooster, hen and chicks in 'contending colours', the most famous of Ming porcelains.
description: The Chenghua emperor's imperial wares are small and delicate, and the chicken cups, only about eight centimetres across, are the most celebrated. Their decoration combines two techniques: outlines painted in underglaze cobalt blue and fired, then filled with overglaze enamels in red, yellow and green and fired again, a method called doucai, contending or fitting colours. On the cups a rooster and hen with chicks peck among rocks and flowers, a symbol of family harmony. Later emperors, including Yongzheng and Qianlong, had them copied, and even in the Ming they were expensive collectors' items. Very few are known, and one sold in 2014 for about 36 million US dollars.
image_file: 明成化 景德鎮窯鬥彩雞缸杯-Chicken Cup MET 1987 85 2015AT 001 (cropped).jpg
image_caption: Chicken cup with Chenghua mark, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Carved red lacquer of the Yongle period
creator: chinese-imperial-workshops
type: Carved cinnabar lacquer on wood
location: Palace Museum, Beijing; Victoria and Albert Museum, London; and other collections
note: Dozens of layers of red lacquer carved into deep peonies, the classic product of the early Ming imperial lacquer workshop.
description: Lacquer, the sap of the lacquer tree, hardens into a waterproof, durable film, and Chinese craftsmen had used it since the Neolithic. In carved lacquer (tihong), dozens or even hundreds of thin coats, each dried and polished, are built up on a wooden core and then carved in relief. The imperial Orchard Factory in Beijing, staffed by craftsmen from the south, produced dishes, boxes and cup-stands of extraordinary quality in the Yongle and Xuande reigns, often with large peonies, camellias or landscapes, the reign mark incised and filled with gold. The deep, rounded carving and polished edges are typical of early Ming work. Such pieces were given as diplomatic gifts to Japan and other states and greatly influenced Japanese lacquer.
image_file: WLA vanda Box Carved lacquer on wood Yongle reign period.jpg
image_caption: Carved red lacquer box, Yongle period, Victoria and Albert Museum

title: Cypress Trees
creator: kano-eitoku
type: Eight-panel folding screen, ink, colour and gold on paper
note: A gigantic, twisting cypress spread across gold leaf, the boldest surviving example of Kanō Eitoku's monumental style.
description: This screen was originally a set of sliding doors, probably for the palace of Prince Hachijō no Miya Toshihito in Kyoto, built in 1590, the year of Eitoku's death; it was later remounted as a screen. A huge cypress tree twists across the panels, its trunk and branches thrusting out of the frame, with blue water and rocks below and gold clouds and ground behind. The scale and energy of the tree express the power and ambition of the Momoyama warlords whose castles Eitoku decorated. Though some scholars attribute it partly to his workshop, it is regarded as the most important surviving work in his style and is a National Treasure.
image_file: 狩野永徳《檜図屏風》1590年、16世紀、桃山時代、東京国立博物館.jpg
image_caption: Kanō Eitoku, Cypress Trees, 1590

title: Scenes in and around Kyoto (Uesugi screens)
creator: kano-eitoku
type: Pair of six-panel folding screens, ink, colour and gold on paper
note: A bird's-eye panorama of Kyoto with some 2,500 figures, given by Oda Nobunaga to the warlord Uesugi Kenshin.
description: Screens of scenes in and around the capital (rakuchū rakugai zu) were a popular genre in the sixteenth century, showing Kyoto's palaces, temples, streets and festivals seen from above through gaps in golden clouds. This pair, painted by the young Kanō Eitoku, is the most celebrated. According to tradition it was commissioned by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiteru and later presented by Oda Nobunaga to Uesugi Kenshin in 1574. It includes the shogun's palace, the Gion festival procession, merchants, priests, samurai and townspeople at work and play, about 2,500 figures in all. It is a key historical record of Kyoto and a National Treasure.
image_file: Kanō Eitoku - Rakuchū rakugai zu (Uesugi) - right screen.jpg
image_caption: Uesugi Rakuchū rakugai zu, right screen

title: Pine Trees (Shōrin-zu byōbu)
creator: hasegawa-tohaku
type: Pair of six-panel folding screens, ink on paper
note: Groups of pines appearing and vanishing in mist, painted in ink alone, the most celebrated Japanese ink painting.
description: On two six-panel screens, pine trees stand in clusters across empty paper, some dark and close, others pale and fading, so that mist seems to fill the space between them, with a faint mountain in the distance. Tōhaku painted them with a rough brush, perhaps made of straw, in swift wet and dry strokes. The paper is relatively coarse, and the panels seem to have been arranged in an unusual order, leading some scholars to suggest they were preliminary drafts. The screens echo the misty landscapes of Muqi, whom Tōhaku admired, but evoke a Japanese coastal landscape. They are a National Treasure and often called the masterpiece of Japanese ink painting.
image_file: Hasegawa Tohaku - Pine Trees (Shōrin-zu byōbu) - right hand screen.jpg
image_caption: Hasegawa Tōhaku, Pine Trees, right screen

title: Crane Scroll (Tsuru shita-e waka kan)
creator: honami-koetsu
type: Handscroll, ink, gold and silver on paper
note: Sōtatsu's gold and silver cranes rise and settle along a 13-metre scroll, overwritten with classical poems in Kōetsu's calligraphy.
description: In this collaboration, Tawaraya Sōtatsu painted flocks of cranes in gold and silver pigments across a long scroll of paper, starting with birds standing on the shore, then rising, flying in long lines and finally landing again. Over this underpainting Hon'ami Kōetsu wrote thirty-six waka poems by the Thirty-six Immortal Poets of the Heian period, his characters swelling and thinning in rhythm with the flight of the birds. The partnership revived the Heian practice of writing poetry on decorated paper but with a new boldness of scale and abstraction. The scroll, nearly fourteen metres long, is an Important Cultural Property and a founding work of Rinpa.

title: Wind God and Thunder God (Fūjin Raijin-zu)
creator: tawaraya-sotatsu
type: Pair of two-panel folding screens, ink, colour and gold on paper
location: Kennin-ji, Kyoto (on deposit at Kyoto National Museum)
note: The green wind god and white thunder god burst across empty gold, Sōtatsu's most famous design and the emblem of Rinpa.
description: On the right screen the green-skinned Wind God rushes in, holding a billowing bag of wind; on the left the white Thunder God beats a ring of drums. Both ride dark clouds painted with tarashikomi, the pooling technique Sōtatsu favoured, and both are pushed to the outer edges, so that the vast empty gold between them seems charged with energy. The figures derive from Buddhist guardian imagery and perhaps from a Kamakura scroll Sōtatsu restored. The screens, which belong to the Zen temple Kennin-ji, are a National Treasure. Ogata Kōrin copied them, and Sakai Hōitsu copied Kōrin's version, making the composition the signature of the Rinpa lineage.
image_file: Wind God and Thunder God Screens by Tawaraya Sotatsu hi-res.png
image_caption: Tawaraya Sōtatsu, Wind God and Thunder God

title: Irises (Kakitsubata-zu)
creator: ogata-korin
type: Pair of six-panel folding screens, colour on gold leaf
note: Clumps of blue-violet irises repeated across a field of gold, an allusion to a famous episode in The Tales of Ise.
