description: In The Tales of Ise, a tenth-century poem tale, a nobleman exiled from the capital stops at a place called Yatsuhashi, the eight bridges, where irises bloom by a stream, and composes a poem whose lines begin with the syllables of the word kakitsubata, iris, mourning the wife he has left behind. Kōrin left out the bridges, the stream and the travellers and painted only the flowers, in clumps of ultramarine and green on gold, rising and falling in a rhythm like music. Some groups are repeated almost exactly, perhaps using stencils, an idea from textile design. The screens are a National Treasure and among the most famous Japanese paintings.
image_file: KORIN-Irises-R.jpg
image_caption: Ogata Kōrin, Irises, right screen

title: Red and White Plum Blossoms (Kōhakubai-zu)
creator: ogata-korin
type: Pair of two-panel folding screens, colour and gold on paper
note: Two plum trees flank a stylised stream of swirling patterns, Kōrin's last great masterpiece.
description: On the left screen an old white plum bends in from the edge, on the right a young red plum rises, and between them a dark, swelling stream flows down, covered with rhythmic swirls that look almost like textile patterns. The trunks are painted with tarashikomi, the pooling ink technique of Sōtatsu, while the stream is thought to have been painted in silver that has darkened, with the swirls left reserved, though the technique has been debated. The contrast between the naturalistic trees and the abstract water, and between old and young, gives the screens a tense balance. Painted late in Kōrin's life, they are a National Treasure.
image_file: Ogata Korin - RED AND WHITE PLUM BLOSSOMS (National Treasure) - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: Ogata Kōrin, Red and White Plum Blossoms

title: Colorful Realm of Living Beings (Dōshoku sai-e)
creator: ito-jakuchu
type: Set of thirty hanging scrolls, colour on silk
location: Museum of the Imperial Collections (Sannomaru Shōzōkan), Tokyo
note: Thirty scrolls of roosters, phoenixes, fish, insects and flowers in jewel-like colour, painted for a Kyoto Zen temple.
description: Over about ten years Itō Jakuchū painted thirty large scrolls of birds, animals, fish, insects, shells and plants, and donated them with a triptych of the Buddha Shaka and two bodhisattvas to Shōkoku-ji, where they were hung for memorial ceremonies, representing all living beings gathered round the Buddha. Each scroll is dense with minutely observed detail: roosters with fiery combs, peacocks and phoenixes with white feathers painted in layers, and fish swimming in shoals. Jakuchū used the finest pigments and sometimes painted on the back of the silk to modulate colour. The temple gave the scrolls to the imperial household in 1889, and they were designated National Treasures in 2021.
image_file: Itō Jakuchū - Black rooster and nandin (Colorful Realm of Living Beings).jpg
image_caption: Black Rooster and Nandina, from the Colorful Realm of Living Beings

title: Pine Trees in Snow (Sesshō-zu)
creator: maruyama-okyo
type: Pair of six-panel folding screens, ink and gold on paper
note: Snow-laden pines rendered almost without outline, the white snow formed by the unpainted paper, Ōkyo's masterpiece.
description: Two great pines, one bent and one upright, stand on the two screens against a ground of gold. The snow lying on their branches is simply the white of the paper left blank, while the needles and bark are painted around it in ink with strokes that model form rather than outline it, and a faint sprinkle of gold dust suggests cold light. Ōkyo developed this method from long study of nature and Western-style shading. The screens were painted for the Mitsui merchant family, important patrons of Ōkyo, and are a National Treasure, the defining work of the Maruyama school's naturalism.
image_file: Okyo Pines right.jpg
image_caption: Maruyama Ōkyo, Pine Trees in Snow, right screen

title: Ten Conveniences and Ten Pleasures (Jūben jūgi-zu)
creator: ike-no-taiga
type: Album of twenty leaves, ink and colour on paper (with Yosa Buson)
note: An album of the joys of country life, Taiga painting the conveniences and Buson the pleasures, a landmark of Japanese literati painting.
description: The Chinese playwright Li Yu wrote poems on the ten conveniences and ten pleasures of his country retreat, and in 1771 a patron commissioned the two leading Japanese literati painters to illustrate them. Ike no Taiga painted the conveniences, such as farming, fishing, drawing water and walking, in a light, humorous style with rounded forms and dots, while Yosa Buson, also the great haiku poet, painted the pleasures of the seasons and weather in a more atmospheric, poetic manner. The album, owned by the novelist Kawabata Yasunari, is a National Treasure and shows how Japanese painters reinvented Chinese literati ideals.

title: Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land (Mongyu dowondo)
creator: an-gyeon
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A painting of Prince Anpyeong's dream of the paradise of Tao Yuanming's fable, the founding masterpiece of Joseon landscape.
description: Prince Anpyeong dreamed in 1447 that he wandered with friends through mountains into a hidden valley of peach blossoms, the paradise described by the Chinese poet Tao Yuanming. He asked An Gyeon to paint it, and the painter finished in three days. Unusually, the scroll reads from left to right: from the ordinary world at the lower left, the viewer passes through craggy, twisting mountains in the Guo Xi manner to the peach blossom valley on the right, shown from above. The prince and twenty-one scholars added inscriptions, making the scroll a document of the brilliant court culture of King Sejong's reign. Taken to Japan, probably during the invasions of the 1590s, it is an Important Cultural Property of Japan and has been shown in Korea only briefly.
image_file: Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land.jpg
image_caption: An Gyeon, Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land

title: Inwangsan after Rain (Inwang jesaekdo)
creator: jeong-seon
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
note: The granite peaks of Inwangsan in Seoul emerging from mist after rain, painted by the 75-year-old Jeong Seon.
description: Mount Inwang rises on the western side of Seoul, and Jeong Seon grew up beneath it. In the summer of 1751, after a week of rain, he painted the mountain as it emerged from the clouds. The great bare granite cliffs are painted with heavy, dark ink in broad horizontal strokes, contrasted with mist rising from the valleys and pines and houses at the base. Many scholars believe it was painted for his lifelong friend, the poet Yi Byeong-yeon, who was gravely ill and died days later, and see it as a prayer for his recovery. Long in the Samsung collection, it was donated to the National Museum of Korea in 2021. It is a National Treasure and the most famous true-view landscape.
image_file: Inwangjesaekdo.jpg
image_caption: Jeong Seon, Inwangsan after Rain, 1751

title: Complete View of the Diamond Mountains (Geumgang jeondo)
creator: jeong-seon
type: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on paper
note: The twelve thousand peaks of Korea's Diamond Mountains gathered into a single circle of crystal spikes and green hills.
description: The Diamond Mountains in present-day North Korea were famous for their many granite pinnacles, and Jeong Seon travelled there several times. In this painting he shows the whole inner range as if from above, in a round, almost cosmic composition: the sharp white peaks on the right are drawn with vertical lines, while the earthy, forested hills on the left are rendered with soft, wet dots. The two halves have been read as yin and yang. An inscription describes the mountain range. Rather than following a Chinese model, the work captures the character of a real Korean landscape. It is National Treasure No. 217.
image_file: Geumgangjeondo.jpg
image_caption: Jeong Seon, Complete View of the Diamond Mountains, 1734

title: Album of Genre Paintings (Danwon pungsokdo cheop)
creator: kim-hong-do
type: Album of 25 leaves, ink and light colour on paper
note: Twenty-five scenes of everyday Joseon life, from wrestling matches and a village school to blacksmiths and dancers.
description: Each leaf of the album shows a scene of ordinary life without background: a ring of spectators watching two men wrestle (ssireum), a boy crying in front of his teacher while classmates laugh, a smithy, women washing clothes, men threshing grain, a dancer and musicians. Kim Hong-do drew with quick, confident outlines and light colour, and he had an eye for gesture, humour and composition, arranging figures in circles or diagonals. The scenes reflect the interest in real Korean life of eighteenth-century Joseon culture. The attribution of every leaf to Kim himself has been questioned, but the album, Treasure No. 527, is one of the most beloved works of Korean art.
image_file: Danwon Ssireum.jpg
image_caption: Ssireum (wrestling), from Kim Hong-do's album

title: Portrait of a Beauty (Miindo)
creator: shin-yun-bok
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A full-length portrait of a young woman in a voluminous skirt, holding the ribbons of her jacket: the classic image of Joseon beauty.
description: A young woman, perhaps a gisaeng entertainer, stands facing the viewer, her head with its large braided wig bowed slightly, holding a tassel of a norigae ornament. Her short jacket and full indigo skirt are rendered with delicate lines and soft colour, and her expression is shy and thoughtful. Shin Yun-bok's inscription says that he painted the spring feelings in her heart. Women were rarely the subject of full portraits in Joseon painting, which makes the work unusual. It is in the Kansong Art Museum, founded by the collector Jeon Hyeong-pil, and is a Treasure of Korea.
image_file: Hyewon-Miindo.jpg
image_caption: Shin Yun-bok, Portrait of a Beauty

title: Lovers under the Moon (Wolha jeongin)
creator: shin-yun-bok
type: Album leaf, ink and colour on paper (from Hyewon's album of genre paintings)
note: A secret meeting at midnight under a crescent moon, from Shin Yun-bok's album of genre scenes.
description: A young man with a lantern and a woman in a long veil-like cloak meet beside a wall in a quiet alley at night, under a thin moon. The inscription says that at midnight under a dim moon only the two of them know their hearts. The scene belongs to Shin Yun-bok's album of thirty genre paintings, National Treasure No. 135, which shows the amusements, flirtations and festivals of the Seoul elite and gisaeng. The fine line, bright colours and settings in gardens and streets distinguish his elegant style from the rustic humour of Kim Hong-do.
image_file: Hyewon-Wolha.jeongin-3.jpg
image_caption: Shin Yun-bok, Lovers under the Moon

title: Self-portrait
creator: yun-du-seo
type: Ink and light colour on paper
note: A frontal, unflinching self-portrait in which only the face and flaming beard are shown: a masterpiece of Korean portraiture.
description: Yun Du-seo's self-portrait shows his face alone, frontal, with intense, staring eyes and a large beard painted hair by hair, floating on the paper without a body. Infrared and X-ray studies have shown that ears and the outline of a robe and body were originally drawn in faint lines that have since faded, so its striking appearance is partly due to time. The work reflects Joseon portraiture's ideal of conveying the spirit through exact likeness. Painted by a scholar barred from office, it has been read as a gaze of self-scrutiny. It is National Treasure No. 240.
image_file: Yun Du-seo.jpg
image_caption: Yun Du-seo, Self-portrait

title: Sehando (Winter Scene)
creator: kim-jeong-hui
type: Handscroll, ink on paper
note: A bare house between pines and cypresses in winter, painted in exile on Jeju for a loyal pupil, the purest Korean literati painting.
description: While Kim Jeong-hui was in exile on Jeju Island, his former interpreter-pupil Yi Sang-jeok, who travelled to Beijing with embassies, kept sending him rare books from China at great trouble. In gratitude Kim painted this scene in 1844, alluding to Confucius's saying that only when the year grows cold do we see that pine and cypress are the last to fade. A simple house stands between four bare trees on an empty ground, drawn with dry, sparse strokes. Yi took it to Beijing, where sixteen Qing scholars added colophons. The scroll was in Japan in the twentieth century, saved during the war by the calligrapher Son Jae-hyeong, and donated to the National Museum in 2020. It is National Treasure No. 180.
image_file: Sehando.jpg
image_caption: Kim Jeong-hui, Sehando, 1844

title: Moon jar
creator: joseon-potters
type: White porcelain
location: Leeum Museum of Art, Seoul; National Museum of Korea; British Museum and others
note: A large, softly asymmetrical white porcelain jar named for its resemblance to the full moon.
description: Moon jars were made at the official kilns of Gwangju near Seoul from the late seventeenth to the mid eighteenth century, a time when Joseon taste favoured plain white porcelain. Because they are so large, often around 40 centimetres high, they were made in two hemispherical halves joined at the middle, so that each is slightly uneven, and the milky glaze varies in colour from bluish to creamy. Their exact use is unclear, perhaps for storing food or as display pieces. Their unpretentious, natural beauty was celebrated by twentieth-century Korean painters and Western potters such as Bernard Leach, and the moon jar has become a symbol of Korean aesthetics. Several are National Treasures.
image_file: 백자 달항아리(309호).jpg
image_caption: Moon jar, National Treasure No. 309

title: Fish and Rocks
creator: bada-shanren
type: Handscroll or album leaves, ink on paper
location: Cleveland Museum of Art (and other collections)
note: Fish with glaring eyes floating in empty space beside precarious rocks, the hallmark of Bada Shanren's strange, compressed style.
description: Bada Shanren painted fish many times, usually without water: a single fish or a pair hang in the blank paper, their round eyes rimmed in black and turned upward with what seems like suspicion or disdain. Rocks above them are top-heavy and seem about to topple, and birds perch on one leg. A few strokes of ink, wet and dry, create each form. His inscriptions, often cryptic, play on classical texts. Whether the images are coded expressions of loyalty to the fallen Ming and contempt for the Qing is debated, but their wit and isolation are unmistakable. His radical economy influenced many modern painters, including Qi Baishi and Zhang Daqian.
image_file: Bada Shanren (Chinese, 1626-1705) - Fish and Rocks - 1953.247 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
image_caption: Bada Shanren, Fish and Rocks, Cleveland Museum of Art

title: Reminiscences of Qinhuai River
creator: shitao
type: Album of eight leaves, ink and colour on paper
note: An album recalling Shitao's travels around Nanjing, in which a monk bows before a cliff that bows back.
description: Shitao lived in Nanjing for several years in the 1680s, and this album recalls places along the Qinhuai River and around the city in eight leaves, each with a poem. The most famous shows a small figure in a boat bowing to a great overhanging cliff that seems to lean towards him, a humorous image of the bond between the artist and nature. Other leaves show plum blossoms, river villages and rocks in fresh colour and free, varied brushwork. The album shows Shitao's insistence, in his treatise on painting, on finding his own method and expressing direct experience rather than copying the old masters.
image_file: Shitao-Qinhuai.jpg
image_caption: Shitao, leaf from Reminiscences of Qinhuai River

title: The Kangxi Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour, Scroll Three
creator: wang-hui
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
note: One of twelve giant scrolls recording the Kangxi Emperor's tour of the south in 1689, directed by Wang Hui.
description: In 1689 the Kangxi Emperor made his second tour of inspection of southern China, travelling down the Grand Canal to Hangzhou and Shaoxing. To commemorate it, the court commissioned twelve handscrolls, each about 70 centimetres high and up to 26 metres long, from a team led by Wang Hui. Scroll Three, in the Metropolitan Museum, follows the emperor from Jinan in Shandong to the sacred Mount Tai, with towns, markets, fields and crowds observed in detail. The project combined the Orthodox school's landscape tradition with documentary record and imperial propaganda. Several of the twelve scrolls survive in Beijing, Paris and New York, and they set the pattern for Qianlong's later tour scrolls.
image_file: 清 王翬 等 康熙南巡圖 （卷三- 濟南至泰山） 卷-The Kangxi Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour, Scroll Three- Jinan to Mount Tai MET DP105303 CRD.jpg
image_caption: Southern Inspection Tour, Scroll Three (section), Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: One Hundred Horses
creator: castiglione
type: Handscroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A hundred horses grazing, rolling and bathing in a wide landscape, combining European perspective and shading with Chinese format.
description: Castiglione painted this long handscroll for the Yongzheng Emperor, and a preparatory drawing for it is in the Metropolitan Museum. It shows a herd of a hundred horses with grooms in an open landscape of willows and pines, some grazing, some rolling on the ground or being driven to a river. The horses are modelled in light and shade with European anatomy and foreshortening, and the landscape recedes towards a low horizon in one-point perspective, but there are no strong cast shadows and the painting is on silk in Chinese pigments, so that it could please Chinese eyes. The work is a classic example of the hybrid court style of the eighteenth century and became one of Castiglione's most famous paintings.
image_file: One Hundred Horses (part1).jpg
image_caption: Castiglione, One Hundred Horses (section)

title: The Qianlong Emperor in Ceremonial Armour on Horseback
creator: castiglione
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on silk
note: The young Qianlong Emperor in gold-studded armour on a white horse, reviewing his troops, in Castiglione's hybrid style.
description: This large portrait shows the Qianlong Emperor in the armour he wore for the grand review of troops at Nanyuan, riding a prancing white horse in a landscape, holding a bow. The emperor's face is painted frontally with soft European modelling but no strong shadows, in accordance with Chinese taste, and the details of armour and harness are exact. The date is debated, with 1739 and 1758 both proposed. The image has become one of the best-known portraits of a Chinese emperor and represents the Manchu ideal of the ruler as a warrior on horseback, central to Qianlong's self-image.
image_file: The Qianlong Emperor in Ceremonial Armour on Horseback.jpg
image_caption: Castiglione, The Qianlong Emperor in Ceremonial Armour on Horseback

title: Famille rose porcelain
creator: jingdezhen-potters
type: Porcelain with overglaze enamels
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; Palace Museum, Beijing; and many other collections
note: Porcelain painted with soft, opaque pink and other enamels developed in the Qing court in the 1720s, inspired by European enamels.
description: In the late Kangxi reign, the Qing court's enamel workshops, with the help of European missionaries, learned to make an opaque pink enamel derived from colloidal gold, together with an opaque white that could be mixed with other colours to create a range of soft shades. Applied over the glaze on Jingdezhen porcelain and fired again at low temperature, these enamels allowed painting with modelling and gradation, like painting on paper. Western collectors called the wares famille rose; Chinese terms include fencai and falangcai. The Yongzheng period produced the most refined examples, and under Qianlong famille rose was used for virtuoso vases and for export porcelain made for Europe in huge quantities.
image_file: 清中期 景德鎮窯粉彩子母雞盤-Dish with Rooster, Hen, and Chickens MET LC-79 2 577 001.jpg
image_caption: Famille rose dish with rooster, hen and chicks, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Jadeite Cabbage
creator: chinese-imperial-workshops
type: Jadeite carving
note: A piece of jadeite carved into a bok choy cabbage with two insects, the most popular object in the National Palace Museum.
description: The carving, about 19 centimetres long, uses a single piece of jadeite that shades from white to green; the carver made the white part the stem and the green part the leaves of a Chinese cabbage, with a locust and a katydid hiding in the leaves. The flaws and cracks in the stone became the veins of the leaves. The cabbage is thought to have belonged to the Guangxu Emperor's consort Jin, perhaps as part of her dowry, symbolising purity, with the insects suggesting fertility. It was displayed in the Forbidden City and later evacuated with the imperial collections to Taiwan. The carver is unknown. It is a favourite of visitors to the museum and a symbol of Qing virtuoso craftsmanship.
image_file: Jadeite Cabbage, National Palace Museum.jpg
image_caption: Jadeite Cabbage, National Palace Museum, Taipei

title: Beauty Looking Back (Mikaeri bijin-zu)
creator: hishikawa-moronobu
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on silk
note: A young woman in a red kimono turns to glance over her shoulder, the defining image of the early ukiyo-e beauty.
description: A woman walks to the left, then turns her head to look back, revealing the fashionable obi tied in a high knot and the floral pattern of her bright red kimono. The pose shows off the clothes and the elegant line of her body. The painting is unsigned except for a seal and an inscription reading 'Hishikawa Moronobu', which some scholars think may be of a pupil. As a painting, not a print, it was more expensive and made for a wealthy client. The image became one of the icons of Japanese art and appeared on a famous postage stamp of 1948.

title: Girl Viewing Plum Blossoms at Night
creator: suzuki-harunobu
type: Polychrome woodblock print (nishiki-e)
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
note: A girl holding a lantern looks at white plum blossoms in the dark garden, a poetic early masterpiece of the colour print.
description: On a veranda, a young woman leans forward with a paper lantern to see a branch of white plum blossom in the night, while a maid looks on. The background is a uniform black, an unusual and difficult effect in woodblock printing, and the blossoms are left in the white of the paper with blind-embossing for texture. Harunobu's figures are slender and delicate, and the scene evokes classical poems about plum blossoms whose scent is noticed at night. It belongs to the first years of the full-colour brocade print, which Harunobu pioneered in 1765.
image_file: Suzuki Harunobu - Woman Admiring Plum Blossoms at Night.jpg
image_caption: Suzuki Harunobu, Girl Viewing Plum Blossoms at Night

title: Three Beauties of the Present Day
creator: utamaro
type: Woodblock print, ink, colour and mica
location: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (and other impressions)
note: Three famous Edo beauties of 1793 in a single print, their faces subtly distinguished, the classic image of Utamaro's art.
description: The print shows three young women celebrated in Edo in 1793: Tomimoto Toyohina, a geisha of the Yoshiwara, at the top, with Takashima Hisa and Naniwa Kita, daughters of tea shop owners, below, each identified by a crest on her kimono. Their faces look very similar at first, but on close inspection their features and expressions differ. The background is dusted with mica, giving a shimmer. The print is a remarkable example of the ōkubi-e, big-head picture, which Utamaro developed and which concentrated on the face. Such prints functioned partly as celebrity images. It became famous in Europe in the nineteenth century.
image_file: Utamaro (1793) Three Beauties of the Present Time, MFAB 21.6382.jpg
image_caption: Utamaro, Three Beauties of the Present Day, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

title: Woman Blowing a Poppin (from Ten Types of Women's Physiognomy)
creator: utamaro
type: Woodblock print, ink, colour and mica
note: A young woman in a chequered kimono blows a glass toy, one of Utamaro's first large-head portraits.
description: The series Ten Types of Women's Physiognomy, published by Tsutaya Jūzaburō, presented types of character through faces, a playful use of the fashionable pseudo-science of physiognomy. In this print a young townswoman in a red and white chequered kimono turns to blow into a poppin, a glass toy that clicks when air is blown into it. The background is covered with glittering white mica. The drawing of hair, skin and fabric is refined, and the woman's absorbed expression gives a sense of a real moment. The print is among the earliest and most famous ōkubi-e.
image_file: 婦女人相十品 相観歌麿考画-Woman with a Glass Noisemaker (Popen) MET DP135591.jpg
image_caption: Utamaro, Woman Blowing a Poppin, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Ōtani Oniji III as Yakko Edobei
creator: sharaku
type: Woodblock print, ink, colour and dark mica
location: Tokyo National Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art and other collections
note: A kabuki villain with claw-like hands and a twisted mouth, the most famous of Sharaku's actor prints.
description: In the fifth month of 1794, the actor Ōtani Oniji III played Edobei, a henchman who robs another character, in the play The Colourful Reins of a Loving Wife at the Kawarazaki theatre. Sharaku's portrait shows him at a moment of menace, eyes narrowed, mouth pressed into a frown, hands thrust forward with splayed fingers. The dark mica background makes the figure stand out. The exaggeration of features, almost caricature, captures the intensity of the actor's performance. The print belongs to Sharaku's first series of 28 bust portraits, published by Tsutaya Jūzaburō, and is now one of the most recognised Japanese prints.
image_file: Toshusai Sharaku- Otani Oniji, 1794.jpg
image_caption: Sharaku, Ōtani Oniji III as Yakko Edobei, 1794

title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
creator: hokusai
type: Polychrome woodblock print
location: Many impressions, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, British Museum and Tokyo National Museum
note: A colossal wave curls over three boats with Mount Fuji small in the distance: the most famous image in Japanese art.
description: The Great Wave is the first print in Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published by Nishimuraya Yohachi from about 1830. A huge wave with claw-like foam rears up over three narrow boats of rowers, while far away Mount Fuji appears as a small cone, echoing the shape of a smaller wave in the foreground. The composition, read from right to left in Japanese style, uses Western-style low horizon and perspective, and the print was one of the first to use the imported synthetic pigment Prussian blue. Thousands of impressions were printed. It reached Europe in the later nineteenth century, inspiring Debussy and many artists, and has become a global icon.
image_file: Tsunami by hokusai 19th century.jpg
image_caption: Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa

title: Fine Wind, Clear Morning (Red Fuji)
creator: hokusai
type: Polychrome woodblock print
location: Many impressions, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and British Museum
note: Mount Fuji glowing red in the early autumn morning against a sky of fish-scale clouds.
description: Also from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, this print shows the mountain alone, its slopes red in the light of a late summer or early autumn morning when a south wind blows, as the title suggests. The summit still has streaks of snow, the base is dark green with forest, and the sky is filled with rows of small clouds. The print is one of the simplest and boldest in the series, reducing the landscape to a few areas of colour. Early impressions have a soft gradation of colour that later ones lost. With the Great Wave and the Thunderstorm below the Summit, it is one of the three most famous prints of the series.
image_file: 「富嶽三十六景 凱風快晴」-South Wind, Clear Sky (Gaifū kaisei), also known as Red Fuji, from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku sanjūrokkei) MET DP141062.jpg
image_caption: Hokusai, Fine Wind, Clear Morning, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Hokusai Manga
creator: hokusai
type: Woodblock-printed sketchbooks, 15 volumes
note: Fifteen volumes of printed sketches of people, animals, gods, plants and everyday life, a vast encyclopedia of Hokusai's drawing.
description: In 1812 Hokusai visited Nagoya and made hundreds of sketches for his pupils, and in 1814 a local publisher issued the first volume as a guide for students. Its success led to further volumes, the last three published after his death, fifteen in all. They contain thousands of images: wrestlers, bathers, fat and thin people, acrobats, ghosts, animals, plants, landscapes, buildings and tools, printed in black, grey and pink. Manga here means casual or random sketches. The books spread Hokusai's style and reached Europe, where they inspired artists such as Félix Bracquemond and the Impressionists. The term manga is now used for Japanese comics.
image_file: Hokusai-MangaBathingPeople.jpg
image_caption: Bathers, from Hokusai Manga

title: The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō
creator: hiroshige
type: Series of 55 polychrome woodblock prints
note: The series that made Hiroshige famous: travellers, rain, snow and moonlight along the highway between Edo and Kyoto.
description: The Tōkaidō, the main highway along the Pacific coast between Edo and Kyoto, had fifty-three post stations, and travel guides and prints of it were popular. Hiroshige's series, published by Hōeidō and Tsuruya, includes the starting point Nihonbashi, the fifty-three stations and Kyoto, 55 prints in all. They show travellers, porters, palanquins, inns and local people in all kinds of weather: driving rain at Shōno, snow at Kanbara, wind at Yokkaichi. The scenes combine accurate observation with lyrical atmosphere. The series sold in huge numbers, launching the craze for landscape prints, and Hiroshige later made many other Tōkaidō series.
image_file: Utagawa Hiroshige (the first) - Shono from the Fifty-three Stations on Tokaido Highway, Hoeido version - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: Hiroshige, Shōno: Driving Rain

title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
creator: hiroshige
type: Polychrome woodblock print
location: Many impressions, including the Brooklyn Museum and Metropolitan Museum of Art
note: People hurrying across a bridge in a sudden summer downpour, rain shown as fine diagonal lines; copied in oil by Van Gogh.
description: This print belongs to One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, Hiroshige's last great series, published from 1856 to 1859. A wooden bridge over the Sumida River crosses the picture diagonally, seen from above, while figures with umbrellas and straw coats hurry across it. The rain falls in fine lines of two angles, cut by the block carver with great precision, and dark clouds are printed with graded colour. A raft is poled along the grey river and the far shore of Atake fades in the rain. Van Gogh painted a copy of it in 1887, and its composition influenced Western painters' handling of weather and space.
image_file: Utagawa Hiroshige - Evening Shower at Atake and the Great Bridge.jpg
image_caption: Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake

title: Plum Park in Kameido
creator: hiroshige
type: Polychrome woodblock print
location: Many impressions, including the Brooklyn Museum
note: A plum tree's dark branch fills the foreground, with visitors seen beyond; a radical close-up composition copied by Van Gogh.
description: Also from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, the print shows a famous plum garden at Kameido, east of the city, whose old tree called the Sleeping Dragon Plum was a celebrated sight. Hiroshige placed a gnarled branch of the tree across the front of the picture, cut off by the frame, and showed the visitors small behind it under a red sky. This bold use of an enlarged foreground, a device used throughout the series, was new to European viewers. Van Gogh's copy of 1887, painted with a border of invented Japanese characters, is in the Van Gogh Museum.
image_file: De pruimenboomgaard te Kameido-Rijksmuseum RP-P-1956-743.jpeg
image_caption: Hiroshige, Plum Park in Kameido, Rijksmuseum

title: Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre
creator: kuniyoshi
type: Triptych of polychrome woodblock prints
location: Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and other collections
note: A giant skeleton rears out of a ruined palace to attack a warrior, summoned by a princess-sorceress.
description: The print illustrates a story of Princess Takiyasha, daughter of the tenth-century rebel Taira no Masakado, who lived on in his ruined palace at Sōma and used sorcery to summon spirits. Here she recites a spell from a scroll on the left, while a gigantic skeleton leans over a broken bamboo screen across two sheets of the triptych to attack the warrior Ōya no Mitsukuni and his companion, who are sent to destroy her. Kuniyoshi drew the skeleton with an accuracy that suggests he had studied Western anatomy books. The scale and drama of the composition are typical of his inventive warrior and ghost prints.
image_file: Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre, by Utagawa Kuniyoshi.jpg
image_caption: Kuniyoshi, Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre

title: Shrimps
creator: qi-baishi
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
location: Beijing Fine Art Academy, National Art Museum of China and other collections (many versions)
note: Translucent shrimps painted with a few strokes of ink, Qi Baishi's signature subject.
description: Qi Baishi kept shrimps in a bowl on his desk to observe them and painted them for decades, gradually simplifying his method. A few pale, wet strokes form the body and its segments, a darker spot the head, and fine dry lines the long antennae and legs, so that the creatures seem transparent and alive in water that is never painted. He said that he had changed the way he painted shrimps several times until he reached the form he wanted in his seventies. His shrimps became immensely popular and are among the best-known images in modern Chinese art. Because Qi Baishi died in 1957, his paintings are not reproduced here.

title: Portrait of Wu Changshuo
creator: ren-bonian
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on paper
location: Zhejiang Provincial Museum and other collections (several portraits)
note: Ren Bonian's affectionate portraits of his friend Wu Changshuo, showing the Shanghai school's fresh, lively figure painting.
description: Ren Bonian painted his younger friend Wu Changshuo several times in the 1880s, in moods ranging from formal to humorous: seated in the summer heat with bared chest, holding a hoe as a poor scholar, or dressed in an official's robes. The faces are carefully modelled, sometimes with light shading that may reflect Western influence, while the bodies and clothes are drawn with quick, calligraphic strokes. Wu often added long inscriptions, and the portraits record the friendship between the two leading figures of the Shanghai art world. They are among Ren Bonian's most personal works and show his gift for character.

title: Plum Blossoms
creator: wu-changshuo
type: Hanging scroll, ink and colour on paper
note: Branches of plum painted with the rough, powerful strokes of a seal carver and calligrapher, with a long inscription.
description: Plum blossom, which flowers in late winter, was the emblem of the scholar's endurance, and Wu Changshuo painted it throughout his career. Branches cross the paper diagonally, drawn with thick, dry strokes like characters in the ancient Stone Drum script he had copied for decades, and the blossoms are dotted in pink or red with dark centres. The composition is balanced by a block of inscription and red seal impressions he carved himself. The result unites poetry, calligraphy, painting and seal carving in one work, the ideal of the literati tradition, with a new bold force and bright colour that appealed to the Shanghai public.
image_file: Wu Changshuo - Red plum blossoms and rock - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: Wu Changshuo, Red Plum Blossoms and Rock

title: Horses in ink
creator: xu-beihong
type: Hanging scroll, ink on paper
location: Xu Beihong Memorial Museum, Beijing (and other versions)
note: Xu Beihong's horses, painted in broad, wet ink strokes on Western anatomical principles.
description: Xu Beihong painted horses throughout his life, using his knowledge of anatomy from drawing in Paris and observation of horses in the Central Asian borderlands and in Singapore. In his galloping horses the animal runs with flying mane and tail, often seen in steep foreshortening, the bones and muscles indicated with a few broad, wet strokes and the hooves with sharp touches. During the war against Japan these spirited animals were seen as symbols of the nation's will to resist. They became the most famous of all his works and models for later ink painters.
image_file: Horse Standing by Xu Beihong, 1940.jpg
image_caption: Xu Beihong, Horse Standing, 1940

title: Merciful Mother Kannon (Hibo Kannon)
creator: kano-hogai
type: Hanging scroll, colour on silk
location: Tokyo University of the Arts Museum
note: A luminous Kannon pours the water of life onto a baby floating in a bubble, the founding work of modern nihonga.
description: Kanō Hōgai painted Hibo Kannon in the last months of his life, finishing it just before his death in 1888. The bodhisattva of compassion, Kannon, floats in a golden mist above a dark mountainous landscape, pouring water from a vase onto a newborn child enclosed in a transparent sphere, who looks up at her. The figure combines traditional Buddhist imagery with Western ideas of light and atmosphere and Renaissance images of the Madonna, which Fenollosa had shown Hōgai. The colours are vivid and the space deep. The painting was hailed as the model for the new Japanese painting that Fenollosa and Okakura promoted, and it is an Important Cultural Property.
image_file: Kanō Hōgai - Hibo kannon (Avalokitesvara as a Merciful Mother).jpg
image_caption: Kanō Hōgai, Merciful Mother Kannon, 1888

title: Lakeside (Kohan)
creator: kuroda-seiki
type: Oil on canvas
location: Kuroda Memorial Hall, Tokyo National Museum, Tokyo
note: Kuroda's future wife in a summer kimono, fan in hand, beside Lake Ashi: the best-loved Japanese oil painting of the Meiji era.
description: In the summer of 1897 Kuroda stayed at Hakone and painted Kaneko Teruko, who later became his wife, seated on a rock beside Lake Ashi with a round fan, the water and mountains behind her in pale blue. The painting uses the light palette and soft, natural light of the French plein-air painting he had learned from Raphaël Collin, but the subject, pose and mood are quietly Japanese. It was shown at the Hakubakai exhibition and later at the Paris Exposition of 1900. It is an Important Cultural Property and appeared on a Japanese postage stamp.
image_file: Kuroda-seiki-kohan00-6-1b.jpeg
image_caption: Kuroda Seiki, Lakeside, 1897

title: Jo no mai
creator: uemura-shoen
type: Hanging scroll, colour on silk
location: Tokyo University of the Arts Museum
note: A young woman of good family performs the opening dance of a Noh play, Shōen's most celebrated image of feminine dignity.
description: Jo no mai is the slow introductory dance of a Noh play. Uemura Shōen shows a young woman in a vermilion kimono with a long-sleeved robe, standing still with her fan held forward, her eyes cast down, at the moment of starting the dance. The pure line, refined colours and controlled posture express what Shōen called the dignity and spiritual purity of a woman. It was shown at the government exhibition of 1936 and bought by the government. It is an Important Cultural Property.
image_file: Jo-no-mai by Uemura Shoen.jpg
image_caption: Uemura Shōen, Jo no mai, 1936

title: The Wheel of Life (Seisei ruten)
creator: yokoyama-taikan
type: Handscroll, ink on silk
location: National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo
note: A forty-metre ink scroll following a drop of water from mountain stream to river and sea and back to the clouds.
description: Taikan's longest work, about forty metres long, follows the journey of water: mist in the mountains, a stream in the forest, a river through villages, its broadening to the sea, a storm, and in the end a dragon rising into the clouds, suggesting the cycle of rebirth. It was painted entirely in ink, using the full range of traditional techniques and the hazy washes of Taikan's mōrōtai style. It was exhibited at the Japan Art Institute exhibition that opened on 1 September 1923, the day of the Great Kantō Earthquake, and survived. It is an Important Cultural Property. Because Taikan died in 1958, it is not reproduced here.
museum_name: National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo (MOMAT)

title: Splashed-colour landscapes
creator: zhang-daqian
type: Ink and colour on paper or silk
location: National Palace Museum, Taipei, and other collections
note: Mountains and mists made by pouring ink and mineral colour onto paper, Zhang Daqian's late fusion of Chinese tradition and abstraction.
description: From the early 1960s, while living in Brazil and California and suffering from failing eyesight, Zhang Daqian developed the technique of splashed ink and colour (pomo pocai). He poured ink and brilliant mineral blues and greens onto paper, tilting it so that they flowed and pooled, then added a few houses, trees or boats with a fine brush to turn the abstract forms into misty mountains. The method drew on the Tang painter Wang Mo's legendary splashed ink and on the blue-and-green tradition, but the effect recalled Abstract Expressionism. His last great work, the huge Panorama of Mount Lu (1981–83), is in the National Palace Museum, Taipei. Because Zhang died in 1983, these works are not reproduced here.

title: Electric Dress
creator: tanaka-atsuko
type: Painted light bulbs, electric cords and controller (performance and installation)
note: A wearable sculpture of flashing coloured light bulbs, worn by the artist at the second Gutai Art Exhibition in Tokyo in 1956.
description: Inspired by the neon advertising signs of Osaka, Tanaka Atsuko made a dress of about two hundred light bulbs and tubes painted in bright colours and wired to flash in sequence. She wore it in public at the second Gutai exhibition, describing the risk of electric shock and the heat as part of the experience. The work fused painting, sculpture, performance and technology, and anticipated later installation and body art. Tanaka later painted large canvases of circles connected by lines, based on the dress's wiring diagrams. The original was rebuilt in later decades for exhibitions. Her works are under copyright and are not reproduced here.

title: Infinity Nets
creator: kusama
type: Series of oil paintings on canvas
note: Huge canvases covered with thousands of small looping brushmarks, the paintings with which Kusama made her name in New York.
description: Soon after arriving in New York in 1958, Kusama began painting very large canvases, some more than ten metres long, entirely covered with tiny loops of white paint over a darker ground, repeated obsessively for hours at a time. The nets have no centre or edge and seem to extend beyond the canvas. When shown in 1959 they were praised by critics including Donald Judd and were seen as anticipating Minimalism. Kusama connects the repetition with her hallucinations and the idea of self-obliteration. She has returned to the Infinity Nets throughout her career. Her works are under copyright and are not reproduced here.

title: TV Buddha
creator: nam-june-paik
type: Video installation: Buddha statue, monitor and closed-circuit camera
note: A statue of the Buddha contemplates its own live image on a television screen, a classic of early video art.
description: Nam June Paik first made TV Buddha in 1974 for an exhibition in New York, reportedly to fill a gap in the show. An old seated Buddha statue faces a television monitor, and a closed-circuit video camera behind the monitor films the statue, so that the Buddha sits watching its own image in an endless present. The work brings together Eastern contemplation and Western technology, the ancient and the electronic, and the narcissism of watching oneself on screen. Paik made many later versions. It is one of the defining works of video art. Paik's works are under copyright and are not reproduced here.

title: From Line
creator: lee-ufan
type: Series of paintings, pigment with glue on canvas
location: Lee Ufan Museum, Naoshima, and many collections
note: Rows of vertical blue strokes, each fading as the brush runs dry, recording the time and act of painting.
description: In the From Line series, begun in 1973, Lee Ufan loaded a brush with mineral pigment mixed with animal glue and drew it down the canvas from top to bottom until the paint ran out, then repeated the action beside it. Each line fades from dark to pale, and the canvas fills with parallel strokes like a slow rhythm. The paintings, together with the From Point series, reflect Lee's theory, developed in the context of Mono-ha, of art as an encounter between the artist's act, the material and the space. They are also associated with Korean Dansaekhwa. His works are under copyright and are not reproduced here.

title: The Washing Place
creator: park-soo-keun
type: Oil on canvas
note: Women washing clothes in a stream, painted in Park Soo-keun's rough, stone-like texture of greys and browns.
description: After the Korean War, Park Soo-keun painted the lives of ordinary people around him, especially women at work. In The Washing Place a row of women kneel beside a stream, beating and rinsing laundry. The figures are flattened into simple outlines and set in a shallow space, and the surface is built up of many layers of thick paint, scraped and dried, until it resembles granite, which Park linked to the reliefs of ancient Korean stone carving. The muted palette and the dignity of the women give the painting a quiet, timeless quality. A version of the subject set an auction record for Korean art in 2007. Park's works are under copyright and are not reproduced here.
